title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: The Specialists
summary: The Chicago Bears have a bit of drama in the third phase this offseason, but hopefully, they get it sorted, and the three specialists have smooth sailing all year long. Roster Locks There’s no question that a kicker who can boom field goals from 60+ is a weapon, and these days, there are more than […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - NOVEMBER 16: Cairo Santos #8 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a game winning field goal during the second half of an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have a bit of drama in the third phase this offseason, but hopefully, they get it sorted, and the three specialists have smooth sailing all year long. Roster Locks There’s no question that a kicker who can boom field goals from 60+ is a weapon, and these days, there are more than ever who have a leg big enough to do so. Cairo Santos is not that guy. And that’s okay. He’s still a lock for the 53-man roster. So his range, on a good day, tops out about 55 yards, and at times, the Bears won’t even trot him out there to try those. But I’d much rather see the offense try to convert a 4th-and-2 from around midfield than attempt a long field goal. Besides, Santos has been clutch during his career as a Bear, hitting several tying or go-ahead kicks, and he received three game balls in 2025 for his outstanding performance. The narrative around kicking in Soldier Field has been more prevalent of late, and Santos’ experience in the Windy City matters. This year will be his seventh consecutive in Chicago, and he practices field goals at Soldier Field, so he understands the gusts like a visiting kicker can’t. He’s the most accurate field goal kicker in franchise history, he has the most 50+ field goals in franchise history, and he holds the record for the longest postseason field goal in team history (51 yards) that he set in subfreezing conditions. Tory Taylor arrived with a lot of excitement (for a punter), but thus far, he’s been fine. He did have that Special Teams Player of the Week award as a rookie, but other than that, his punting prowess at Iowa hasn’t shown up as a pro. Last year, he was 13th in yards per punt, and in the categories that require some help from the coverage units, he was 25th in net yards per punt, 6th in touchbacks, and 21st in hitting punts inside the twenty. Taylor does need to do a better job at his directional kicking and his dead-ball punts, but hopefully his use continues to decline as Chicago’s offense continues to improve. A Good Bet To Make It Keep scrolling, we have an honest-to-goodness ‘two-man enter, one-man leave’ battle at long snapper coming up in training camp! Roster Bubble/Practice Squad Bill Zimmerman already broke down the long snapper battle between Luke Elkin and Beau Gardner here , so you can check that out for more detail on these two combatants. And if you think the long snapper battle is the most boring on an NFL roster, then you must not understand the cult-like status long snappers have had around Chicago since the Patrick Mannelly era. Jacob’s tweet below has over a million views! Nobody's talking about the #Bears ' long snapper battle, but I'm excited to see it play out in training camp. Luke Elkin was on the practice squad and snapped to Tory Taylor at Iowa, but Beau Gardner won the Patrick Mannelly Award as the best LS in college. Strong claim for both. pic.twitter.com/l17XwC97F5 — Jacob Infante (@jacobinfante24) July 17, 2026

summary: With the Chicago Bears rookies and quarterbacks reporting to Halas Hall today for training camp, that means we also get a wave of roster moves. The Bears announced that linebacker T.J. Edwards was placed on the Active/Non-Football Injury list. The NFI list is for players who are injured away from the team’s facilities (practice or […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 26: T.J. Edwards #53 of the Chicago Bears celebrates a defensive play with Kyler Gordon #6 during the fourth quarter against the Seattle Seahawks at Soldier Field on December 26, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images With the Chicago Bears rookies and quarterbacks reporting to Halas Hall today for training camp, that means we also get a wave of roster moves. The Bears announced that linebacker T.J. Edwards was placed on the Active/Non-Football Injury list. The NFI list is for players who are injured away from the team’s facilities (practice or games), so this injury is unrelated to Edwards’ broken fibula that he suffered in the Wildcard game. NFL Insider Ian Rapoport reported that it’s a “minor muscle strain” and T.J.‘s stay on the NFI list “should be short.” The Bears also placed rookie linebacker Keyshaun Elliott, nickleback Kyler Gordon, linebacker Noah Sewell, offensive tackle Ozzy Trapilo, and defensive lineman Shemar Turner on the Active/Physically Unable to Perform list. The PUP list is for players who are still rehabbing an injury from football activities. Elliott is dealing with a quad issue; Gordon had some soft-tissue injuries that kept him out this offseason; Sewell tore his Achilles tendon in December; Trapillo is still working back from the ruptured patellar tendon he suffered in the playoffs; and Turner tore his ACL in October. All these players can remain at Halas Hall for meetings and rehab, but they can not practice until medically cleared and removed from the lists. View Link

title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Redacted’s Roster
summary: We have just three more rosters to assess in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. Today, let’s look at Redacted’s roster. Remember, Redacted is either a very important person or someone who is just quite shy and doesn’t want to be a public figure. Either way, they’ve been a member of the league for several […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Rome Odunze #15 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after completing a first down during the second quarter of an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We have just three more rosters to assess in the WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football League. Today, let’s look at Redacted’s roster. Remember, Redacted is either a very important person or someone who is just quite shy and doesn’t want to be a public figure. Either way, they’ve been a member of the league for several years and are a playoff team year in and year out, but they don’t have the playoff success or championships to show for it. They are the Buffalo Bills. Let’s look at the roster: Ironically, we called him the Buffalo Bills when his QB is Josh Allen. Obviously, Allen is a stud and the top QB in fantasy. Love is a great QB2 to have behind Allen. I’d like to see a developmental QB behind these two, but I know he traded Shough (to me) this offseason, so he did have that before trying to use that to strengthen other areas. It’s tough to complain about this running back room. Cook, Jacobs, Hall, and potentially Kamara are all startable backs, and obviously Cook is awesome, and Jacobs and Hall are very good. This is a really solid core. The WR room hasn’t quite come together like I think he hoped it would, but it’s still a very good group. Adams is a point-getter, but for how much longer? Collins is nice. Robinson and Sutton put up points last year, but do I trust them to repeat those types of numbers with some new talent added to those rooms? I do not. Aiyuk has completely derailed. Odunze and Pearsall are good, but haven’t been the point getters many would have expected out of the draft. Having Loveland as your TE1 is a great place to start for your TE room. Schultz is a good TE2. Otton is fine, especially as a TE3. Mayer is interesting to see if he becomes a better receiving threat in a better offense. No complaints here. On the defensive side of the ball, the tackle room is strong. There aren’t a ton of penetrating DTs here; a lot of run stuffers, but they are stuffers that score points. Will Dexter Lawrence bounce back to what he has been? If so, this room is in great shape; if he’s just solid again, the room is good, but without a big-time stud. The Edge room really needs Bain to be a big-time rookie like Jared Verse was a couple of years ago. If Bosa can stay healthy and get back to what he was, that would go a long way. Will Phillips take another step forward in Carolina? That would also help. Certainly a room that needs some love. The linebacker room is also one of the weaker rooms on the team. All 4 linebackers are starters. All of them score, but none of them hoard tackles and score massive points. They all score decent points. Will any of them become that 15 PPG guy that you need at LB? It’ll be interesting to see how this room scores. Redacted has just one CB. He’s a man after my own heart. Well done. The safety room is decent. It’s similar to the LB room. Starting caliber players. They score decent points, but there isn’t a guy that dominates a game and racks up tackles. If Evan Williams or one of the younger guys becomes that, it would certainly elevate the room. The taxi squad has some nice additions. I think all five guys have potential to become contributors on this roster eventually. Trotter could do it this year. This is a very good team. Top to bottom, it might be the most talented offense when you look at all the position groups in the league. However, the defense has a lot of decent guys, but not a lot of big-time point getters. I think if the defense had some more high-end guys, this roster could have won a championship by now.

title: Bear & (NOT) Balanced: Football Festivus – 10 Things We Hate About Football
summary: The NFL is a ratings juggernaut, and they’ve managed to manipulate their yearly schedule to ensure there’s always something to talk about. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The NFL is a ratings juggernaut, and they’ve managed to manipulate their yearly schedule to ensure there’s always something to talk about. For some, the offseason isn’t as newsworthy as the regular season and the playoffs, but you’d be blown away at how many eyes free agency and the draft bring in, at how interested fans are about the 90th man on a 90-man offseason roster, and how the 16-man practice squad is shaping up. Football is the most popular sport in America, and its popularity globally grows every year, but just because we love almost everything about it, that doesn’t mean there aren’t things we can’t stand. Whether that be the way it’s covered, the narratives that drive traffic, the rules, terminology, or any other trivial thing that annoys you, there are things we hate about football. Earlier this week, we asked you guys if there is an NFL-related narrative, topic, or thing that really grinds your gears , and our Chicago Bears fans came through! title: WCG Dynasty Fantasy Football: Assessing Adam Hess’ Roster
summary: It’s Saturday and the Bears report to camp in just a few days. That means next week we are going to be pivoting to a lot of training camp coverage, which means we should wrap up our Dynasty Fantasy Football series this weekend. We have four teams left, so let’s dive in. Adam Hess is […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 18: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears enters the field with his teammates during player introductions prior to an NFL divisional playoff game against the Los Angeles Rams at Soldier Field on January 18, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s Saturday and the Bears report to camp in just a few days. That means next week we are going to be pivoting to a lot of training camp coverage, which means we should wrap up our Dynasty Fantasy Football series this weekend. We have four teams left, so let’s dive in. Adam Hess is the next roster we are going to assess. Adam has been a part of this league for several years, and his team has struggled over the last few years. Let’s see why he isn’t stacking wins and what he can do to improve. Here’s the roster: Let’s break it down, and let’s start with the QB room, where Adam has the best QB room in the league. The problem is, we only start one QB; this is not a Superflex. Adam, trade a quarterback! You’ll never get the value you want out of trading a QB, but Adam arguably has 3 QB1s on the roster, and two of them are on the bench every week. Pick a QB1 (he’ll pick Caleb), trade Stafford to a win-now team, and downgrade Lawrence to a QB2-level QB and maybe pick up an extra pick or another player in the process. At RB, he starts with Jeanty, which is a great spot. I know Jeanty didn’t have the best rookie season, but even with that, he still compiled a pretty strong point total, and he should only improve. This league starts 2 RBs, and there isn’t a viable 2nd starter unless Coleman grabs the bull by the horns in Denver. You can absolutely start Sampson, Dobbins, or maybe even Allgeier in a pinch, but you can’t rely on any of them as an RB2 for a season. The WR room has a lot of guys that are “pretty good.” I feel like this is one of those groups where you try to choose your lineup based on matchups and you inevitably fail to start someone every week that has a strong week. Unless McLaurin finds the magic again this year, this is a roster loaded with WR2s and WR3s that can score a decent number, but there just aren’t any big-time scorers here at an important position. Now we get to the TE room, where again, we argue for the best TE room in the league. Adam has 4 startable TEs; unfortunately, we only start 1 to 2 TEs per week in this league. Make a trade, Adam! There are a lot of teams that have subpar TE rooms, and Adam has at least two to trade. Theo Johnson as your TE5 is also crazy. With the extra talent at TE and QB, you have to wonder why this team isn’t making more trades. Let’s move over to the defense, where Adam has arguably the DT1 in the league in terms of fantasy in Jeffery Simmons. You only have to start 1 DT, but you can start more than that, and Adam used to have Madubuike as a dynamic duo. Can he get back to what he was two years ago? If he does, that changes this room a lot. Payne is solid, but those numbers will probably keep shrinking year over year at this point in his career. The Edge room is strong. Parsons as your top edge is amazing. Byron Young as your DE2 is solid. Scourton going down certainly hurts the depth here, and there isn’t much depth behind those two, but it’s a solid duo as long as it’s healthy. It could certainly use one more Edge that scores more than his other available rotational guys, but he had that potential with Scourton, so tough to criticize less than a week after the injury. The linebacker room is fine, but not spectacular. Cashman scores, but he’s 30, so you proceed with caution there. Overshown needs to recover and prove he can stay healthy, which has always been a challenge for him. Thomas and TooToo are good; perhaps they can improve, but I feel they are the players they will be at this point. Pace is just a guy. The room could use improvement, but it’s also functional and not a major concern. The CB room works; I don’t see Stingley as a guy worth rostering based on CB scoring. The safety room looks really good with Curl and Winfield up top and Moore, Joseph, and Metellus behind them. I like the taxi squad. Simpson is a nice guy to have with Stafford on the roster. Lance and Thomas are nice developmental WRs. Woods and Louis have potential as well. This team needs an RB2 and more high-end WRs, and it’s ready to compete. Without those, this is a middling-low-ceiling team because it doesn’t have enough offensive firepower. With the depth at QB and TE, where he could fix the issues on his roster, you have to wonder what Adam is waiting for.
author: Bill Zimmerman

title: Projecting The Top 3 Defensive Training Camp Battles For The Chicago Bears
summary: In Part 1 of this installment, we focused on the offensive side of the ball. While there isn’t nearly as much angst as we’ve seen in recent years regarding that unit, the defense still has plenty of questions to be answered in the coming weeks. It’s fair to say that with a Top 10-15 defense, […]
full_text: Jan 10, 2026; Chicago, IL, USA; in Chicago Bears defensive end Austin Booker (94) pressures Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love (10) during an NFC Wild Card Round game at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Matt Marton-Imagn Images | Matt Marton-Imagn Images In Part 1 of this installment, we focused on the offensive side of the ball. While there isn’t nearly as much angst as we’ve seen in recent years regarding that unit, the defense still has plenty of questions to be answered in the coming weeks. It’s fair to say that with a Top 10-15 defense, many would consider the Chicago Bears a Super Bowl favorite in the NFC. With plenty of unknowns and existing concerns remaining heading into this season, it’ll take plenty of things to go right for them to take a big leap forward in 2026. Let’s dive into the defensive side of the ball and dissect the Top 3 Training Camp battles to monitor in the coming weeks. Defensive End 2 Heading into the offseason, it was fair to assume the Bears would do something to improve the overall upside of this room. Heading into late July’s start of training camp, this group remains untouched outside of losing Joe Tryon-Shoyinka. In short, the organization is banking on better health, a different coaching style, and growth from younger players to make the improvements needed to join the “Super Bowl Contender” conversation. Call me a skeptic, but for now, it is what it is. Dayo Odeyingbo surprised many when he was a participant in the team’s offseason program. Assuming he doesn’t experience a setback, it appears that their Top 3 edge rushers will be healthy and ready to go for training camp. With Montez Sweat entrenched as their top starting defensive lineman, the competition between Austin Booker and Odeyingbo will be one to monitor closely. Both players had issues staying healthy last year, missing a combined full season between the two. Based on what we saw when both players were healthy, it’s fair to label Booker as the favorite. That said, the coaching staff has acknowledged Odeyingbo’s value on the interior, so don’t be surprised to see all three featured in various obvious pass-rushing situations. Although fans shouldn’t rule out an outside addition in the coming weeks, the team seems confident in its approach to allow the situation to play out, at least into the latter part of the preseason. That means barring a surprise addition, Booker and Odeyingbo will be battling for not only a starting role on the defense but a chance to get to Week 1 healthy. Defensive Tackle Depth Tackle is yet another position that the Bears are hoping they can get more out of, even if the difference in talent between last year and now doesn’t appear to be much different. Last offseason, they gave veteran Grady Jarrett a surprisingly big deal to come over from Atlanta, and for the most part, it did not pan out. With Gervon Dexter Sr. heading into the final year of his rookie deal, the team is hoping the best is yet to come from him. In addition to those two, they added veteran Neville Gallimore to the mix, who should help improve depth and provide more upside than what they got from Andrew Billings in the DT3 spot in 2025. The upside isn’t high from this trio, but the hope is that better scheme fits and another year in the system will be enough to get this group firing off the ball and stopping the run. With those three names locked in, the final spot (or two) will come down to a combination of upside and overall fit. Purely from a numbers game, I’d project five to break camp with the team, but don’t be surprised if the final number is only four. With the sixth-round selection of Jordan van den Berg and veteran minimum signings of Kentavius Street and James Lynch, it feels like a safe bet that the final spots on the depth chart will be settled. With that in mind, Jayden Loving is an undrafted free agent from Wake Forest who, despite his impressive numbers in 2025, was just a one-year college product. None of these names stand out as anything to get overly excited about. Still, it’s clear that the offseason plan focused on scheme fits, which is crucial for Dennis Allen’s defense to operate at its full capabilities. Similar to the defensive end position, it feels like the Bears are counting on a breakout year from someone rather than actually being happy with what they have at both positions. Only time will tell if that gamble pays off. Cornerback 2 In an ideal world, both Jaylon Johnson and Kyler Gordon will stay healthy all year, and CB2 becomes much less of a concern. Although that is not outside the realm of possibility, recent history suggests it might not be worth betting on. Assuming that’s the case, that makes the second starting cornerback spot (and the depth behind them) that much more important. On paper, Tyrique Stevenson is the favorite for the job. The issue for him continues to be consistency and, at times, a lack of confidence. He’s been saying all the right things leading up to camp, but once again, he was getting consistently burned in practice during OTAs and Mini-camp. Maybe the switch will flip once things start getting more competitive, but Bears fans are all too familiar with Stevenson’s inconsistencies throughout his first three years in Chicago. With Nahshon Wright off to New York, they are hoping a combination of fourth-round pick Malik Muhammad and Terell Smith will be enough to keep competition strong. As we’ve learned over the years, banking on a rookie cornerback can be volatile, and even though Smith has shown flashes throughout his three-year NFL career, health and consistency have been lacking. There’s a level of risk heading into camp without a proven veteran option, but it’s easy to see why there’s still confidence in this group. With a healthier year, this group could easily be back in the Top 10 mix. On the flip side, if things trend closer to how they looked in 2025, they’ll need to hope there’s another Wright-level player on the roster who can produce big plays over the course of a long season.
author: Aaron Leming

title: Bryan Cook is coming home to fix the Bengals defense
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals had a huge defensive problem over the past couple of seasons. So when free agency hit, they did not hesitate to land one of the top players at a huge position of need. A player they knew from their own backyard, former Kansas City Chiefs safety Bryan Cook. Bryan Cook Cap Status […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 15: Bryan Cook #6 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates after a play during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Cincinnati Bengals at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium on September 15, 2024 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals had a huge defensive problem over the past couple of seasons. So when free agency hit, they did not hesitate to land one of the top players at a huge position of need. A player they knew from their own backyard, former Kansas City Chiefs safety Bryan Cook. Bryan Cook Height: 6´1¨ Weight: 210 pounds Age: 26 years old College: Cincinnati Hometown: Cincinnati, Ohio Experience: 4 seasons Cap Status Cook signed a three-year contract worth up to $40.25 million with $14 million guaranteed this offseason. He has just over a $10.6 million cap hit this season, according to Over The Cap. He accounts for 3.37 percent of the cap this year and is the 12th highest-paid safety as of writing. Background Most Bengals fans may remember Cook more for the two years he spent at the University of Cincinnati in 2020 and 2021. Especially the 2021 season, when he was part of the team that earned a spot in the College Football Playoffs. He was a first-team All-American Athletic Conference selection that season as well. Bryan Cook is a HUGE upgrade at safety for the Bengals defense. Physical, rangy, dependable tackler, and a great pre-snap communicator. pic.twitter.com/tbj5EyH5fF — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 15, 2026 He was drafted by the Chiefs in the second round of the 2022 draft. He earned a starting role in 2023. He missed the last five games of the 2023 season, but has started every other game since the start of 2024. He has 148 solo tackles, 15 passes defended, three interceptions, and four tackles for a loss over his career. He was the fourth-highest-rated safety at PFF in 2025. A big area of improvement will be that he only missed his tackle 5.6 percent of the time. We will touch on that in the next section as well, though. 2026 Outlook It is hard to see Cook not once again being one of the top safeties in the NFL. It comes as he will be replacing what I will refer to nicely as a poor fit with Geno Stone. Stone was meant to be a ball hawk and create turnovers. Instead, he was a liability at tackling, which Cook is pretty much the opposite of. Bryan Cook highlights starting with some pretty insane range to get outside of the numbers from the opposite hash. Some great processing and anticipation while also showing up as a physical force. pic.twitter.com/Awv40xhLW3 — mike (@bengals_sans) March 9, 2026 Cook is still a great coverage safety. PFF had him ranked as the sixth-highest-rated safety in coverage last year. What Cincinnati fans will notice more of is his ability to get ball carriers down in the open field, which was a rarity among most defenders last season. The underrated aspect Cook should bring is leadership to the defensive side of the ball. He is a guy who has been to the top of the mountain and knows how a championship-winning defense prepares. It is certainly an aspect that side of the ball has needed a bit more of the past couple of years. I mean, sometimes it is that simple: Cook is a premier player at his position. It was a huge position of need for the Bengals. It was a perfect match, and it should play out well for both parties. Signing Bryan Cook in FA was huge. He might end up being an even better signing than Trey Hendrickson was in 2021. Cook earned an 83.5 PFF grade, ranking 4th among safeties. He brings a dynamic we really haven’t had since Jessie Bates. Rangy, versatile, elite attacking… pic.twitter.com/Iai4qXNXIt — 937Bengals 🐅 (@BengalsinDa937) April 15, 2026

title: B.J. Hill and Josh Kattus placed on injury lists to start off Bengals training camp
summary: The Bengals are set to kick off training camp next Wednesday, which means players will be reporting to Cincinnati in the coming days. That also means we’ll see guys placed on various injury lists to start camp, the first being veteran defensive tackle B.J. Hill and rookie tight end Josh Kattus. On Saturday, the Bengals […]
full_text: Dec 16, 2023; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals defensive tackle BJ Hill (92) reacts after sacking Minnesota Vikings quarterback Nick Mullens (not pictured) and picking up the fumble in the first half at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images The Bengals are set to kick off training camp next Wednesday, which means players will be reporting to Cincinnati in the coming days. That also means we’ll see guys placed on various injury lists to start camp, the first being veteran defensive tackle B.J. Hill and rookie tight end Josh Kattus. On Saturday, the Bengals announced that Hill was placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list and Kattus was placed on the Non-Football Injury list. PUP applies to players with football-related injuries, while NFI applies to injuries or illnesses that were sustained away from team activities. It’s unclear what exactly both players are dealing with, so hopefully it’s nothing major that sidelines them for much of training camp. The 31-year-old Hill actually missed the start of camp last year with a foot issue but went on to start all 17 games. Kattus is an undrafted free agent out of Kentucky who is already facing an uphill climb to even make the practice squad, as tight end is one of the deepest positions on the 90-man roster.

title: Jordan Battle is primed to break out next to Bryan Cook
summary: Jordan Battle is a returning starter at safety for the Cincinnati Bengals. After the Bengals added Bryan Cook to play next to him, he should be in line for an even bigger season in 2026. Jordan Battle Contract Status Jordan Battle is entering the 4th season of his 4-year $5,325,000 rookie contract. His base salary […]
full_text: Sep 14, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals safety Jordan Battle (27) celebrates the win after the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Joseph Maiorana-Imagn Images | Joseph Maiorana-Imagn Images Jordan Battle is a returning starter at safety for the Cincinnati Bengals . After the Bengals added Bryan Cook to play next to him, he should be in line for an even bigger season in 2026. Jordan Battle Height: 6´1¨ Weight: 215 pounds Age: 25 years old College: Alabama Hometown: Fort Lauderdale, Florida Experience: 3 seasons Contract Status Jordan Battle is entering the 4th season of his 4-year $5,325,000 rookie contract. His base salary for 2026 is just under $3.7 million. He is scheduled to be an unrestricted free agent after the 2026 season. Overview Battle played his high school football at Florida powerhouse St. Thomas Aquinas. He was selected to the Under Armour All-American game during his senior season. After graduating high school, he chose to continue his football and academic career at Alabama, playing for Coach Nick Saban. He was an immediate contributor early in his career at Alabama. He played in 54 total games, with 44 starts during his four seasons with the Crimson Tide. He finished his career with 251 tackles, 6 interceptions, and 16 passes defensed. He was recognized as a third-team All-American during both his junior and senior seasons. He was also a captain and won a national title with the 2020 team. Battle was selected in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft. After starting 13 games over his first two seasons with the Bengals, Battle started all 17 games in 2025. He led the team with 112 tackles on the season. He had career highs with 6 passes defensed, 2 forced fumbles, and 4 interceptions during the season. Outlook for 2026 Jordan Battle is a returning starter at safety. He will be playing alongside Bryan Cook on the back end of the defense. After the best statistical season of his career, it is expected that Battle will be even better during the 2026 season. After collecting 4 interceptions in 2025, I could see Battle improving upon that number now that the Bengals have a deeper and more talented defensive line to get pressure on the quarterback. The biggest thing for Battle will be to improve on missed tackles. If he can improve that part of his game, this is a player who will cash in during free agency after the season concludes. Jordan Battle should benefit from the addition of Bryan Cook at safety this season. pic.twitter.com/s85hHVpHav — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 19, 2026

title: Bengals struggle in goal-to-go situations under Zac Taylor, despite their insanely talented offense
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have the most talented offense in the NFL. With a top-tier quarterback in Joe Burrow and the league’s best wide receiver duo in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, opposing defenses are often left to pick their poison and hope for the best. So why do they struggle so badly in goal-to-go situations? […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - FEBRUARY 24: Head coach Zac Taylor of the Cincinnati Bengals speaks to the media during the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine at Lucas Oil Stadium on February 24, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have the most talented offense in the NFL. With a top-tier quarterback in Joe Burrow and the league’s best wide receiver duo in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, opposing defenses are often left to pick their poison and hope for the best. So why do they struggle so badly in goal-to-go situations? An offense with this much talent shouldn’t have trouble punching the ball into the end zone after driving the length of the field. Yes, defenses become more condensed inside the 10-yard line, and there’s less space to operate, but that’s hardly enough to justify ranking 24th in the NFL in goal-to-go efficiency . And success in those situations matters. According to Warren Sharp , 74% of all rushing touchdowns are scored from inside the 10-yard line, while 55% of all touchdowns come in goal-to-go situations. The blame doesn’t fall on the players alone. Over the past five seasons, Burrow has been the third-most accurate passer in goal-to-go situations, yet the Bengals rank just 26th in EPA per play (-0.06) and 17th in success rate (44%). With a quarterback that accurate and receivers capable of winning quickly, Cincinnati should be able to spread defenses out and create favorable running lanes near the goal line. Instead, the offense has consistently underperformed in that area. If the Bengals are serious about making a Super Bowl run, that has to change. You can’t settle for chip-shot field goals in the postseason and expect to beat the NFL’s best teams. Cincinnati spent the offseason improving the roster and positioning itself for a deep playoff run. But none of those moves will matter as much if the offense continues leaving points on the field. Whether the defense takes a step forward or not, the Bengals need to turn more of those goal-to-go opportunities into touchdowns. If they’re forced into another season of winning shootouts, the difference between three points and seven could ultimately define how far this team goes.
author: Jason Garrison

title: Where does the “Who Dey!” chant rank among the best NFL team chants?
summary: The “Who Dey!” chant at Bengals games is one of the best parts of being a Bengals fan and a Cincinnati sports fan. When the Ruler of the Jungle leads The Jungle in the Who Dey chant before kickoff, that gets you going as a fan. After a big touchdown, that’s when the “Who Dey!” […]
full_text: A young Cincinnati Bengals fan cheers for the team in the second quarter of a NFL game between the Cincinnati Bengals and Arizona Cardinals, Sunday, Dec. 28, 2025, at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati. | Frank Bowen IV/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The “Who Dey!” chant at Bengals games is one of the best parts of being a Bengals fan and a Cincinnati sports fan. When the Ruler of the Jungle leads The Jungle in the Who Dey chant before kickoff, that gets you going as a fan. After a big touchdown, that’s when the “Who Dey!” chant is at its best. So, where does the chant rank among NFL stadium chants? Sports Illustrated’s Karl Rasmussen ranked the 10 best in the NFL, with the “Who Dey!” chant checking in at No. 6. If you’ve ever wondered how the “Who Dey!” chant came to be, here’s how, according to Rasmussen: The Bengals’ chant originated in 1981, stemming from a popular local car commercial and a beloved beer, Hudepohl. Beer vendors at the team’s former stomping grounds, Riverfront Stadium, used to offer the local beer by shouting “Hudy!” to fans. That eventually transitioned to “Who Dey,” and it evolved further after fans incorporated the song played in commercials by Red Frazier’s Ford of Cincinnati, which goes, “Who’s going to give you a better deal than Red Frazier … nobody!” The combination of both resulted in the Bengals chant. “Who dey? Who dey? Who dey say is gonna beat the Bengals? … Nobody!” Rasmussen also analyzes the comparison between the “Who Dey!” chant in Cincinnati and the “Who Dat!” chant in New Orleans that Saints fans do in the Superdome. In fact, he ranked the “Who Dat!” chant No. 5, one spot above the Bengals. Of course, there’s an ongoing debate between the two teams of which chant came first. One of my favorite memories as a Bengals fan was being at the Bengals-Saints game in New Orleans four years ago. There were so many Bengals fans who made the trip for the game. Before kickoff, Saints fans started doing the “Who Dat!” chant. In response, Bengals fans started doing the “Who Dey!” chant. It was dueling chants, making for an awesome pregame environment. Hopefully there will be many “Who Dey!” chants coming in 2026 at Paycor Stadium, especially against the Saints in Week 12 on Nov. 29, and on the road as well.
author: Alex Frank

title: Joe Flacco earns spot on the 2026 NFL All-Backup Team
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals surprised us all when they traded for Joe Flacco in the middle of the season after Joe Burrow went down last year. The Bengals were crumbling quickly early on last season, but Flacco brought a spark the team, the fanbase, and city desperately needed. Despite a lack of wins, Flacco was incredibly […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco (16) drops back to throw in the second quarter of the NFL Week 11 game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Cincinnati Bengals at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh on Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025. The Steelers led 10-6 at halftime. | Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cincinnati Bengals surprised us all when they traded for Joe Flacco in the middle of the season after Joe Burrow went down last year. The Bengals were crumbling quickly early on last season, but Flacco brought a spark the team, the fanbase, and city desperately needed. Despite a lack of wins, Flacco was incredibly productive in Zac Taylor’s offense thanks to the help of Ja’Marr Chase and is now officially backing up Joe Burrow going into 2026. Bill Barnwell of ESPN recently shared his NFL All-Backup team going into the new season, and Flacco made the roster. “Here’s the veteran in our quarterback room. Flacco, 41, has been effective while bouncing around the league over the past three years, posting a 45.5 QBR while winning games for the Browns, Colts and Bengals. He’s going to throw some truly painful interceptions, but Flacco still has a strong arm, does a solid job of avoiding sacks and can run the offense from under center. He’s a great short-term option for us,” Barnwell wrote. Flacco is the most experienced QB that has been behind Burrow since he was drafted in 2020 and has now shown that he can win in the NFL and win with the offense in Cincinnati, if needed. As hard as it is to say, it is now important to have someone like Flacco behind Burrow after he went down with his third significant injury as a Bengal last year.
author: Patrick Carey

title: Browns: What advice would you give to a new fan?
summary: Kermit the Frog famously said that, “it’s not easy being green.” While that might be true, Kermit has nothing on being a fan of the Cleveland Browns.  The franchise was one of the league’s original dynasties, steamrolling through the NFL in the 1950s behind innovative head coach Paul Brown. But unless you are nearing the […]
full_text: Cleveland Browns fans after Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) is sacked in the fourth quarter of the NFL Week 1 game between the Cleveland Browns and the Cincinnati Bengals at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland on Sunday, Sept. 7, 2025. The Bengals begin the season with a 17-16 win over the Browns. | Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images Kermit the Frog famously said that, “it’s not easy being green.” While that might be true, Kermit has nothing on being a fan of the Cleveland Browns. The franchise was one of the league’s original dynasties, steamrolling through the NFL in the 1950s behind innovative head coach Paul Brown. But unless you are nearing the age of 70, you really don’t have much more than hazy memories of the team’s last NFL Championship in 1964. The Browns had a nice run under head coach Sam Rutigliano and quarterback Brian Sipe in the late 1970s. They went to three AFC Championship Games with quarterback Bernie Kosar operating a talented offense in the late 1980s. But this season marks 40 years since the first of those conference championship game appearances. For fans who have only known the Browns since their return in 1999, they have a handful of talented players – Josh Cribbs, Phil Dawson, Nick Chubb, and Joe Thomas to name a few – and that one playoff win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. Other than that? A seemingly never-ending list of quarterbacks, head coaches, general managers, and seasons of double-digit losses. So why would anyone want to be a fan of this team? That question came to mind while reading about a man in Michigan named John Sparrow who is adopting the Browns as his team, and wrote to cleveland.com columnist Terry Pluto asking for advice on what to expect . Pluto’s response, at least in the written article as he may have expanded on the answer on his Terry’s Talkin’ podcast , was short and to the point: “It teaches you not to have great expectations out of life. Keep those expectations to a minimum.” To be a Browns fan is to have recalibrated your definition of success, Pluto said. A winning season feels like a championship. A playoff appearance is cause for a street celebration. Not to channel Bane from The Dark Knight Rises , but it does feel like you have to be born into being a Browns fan. Because otherwise, why would you sign up for this? That has defined being a Cleveland fan overall for a good part of our lives. The Cavaliers had their “Miracle of Richfield” moment in 1976 before almost moving to Toronto seven years later under the disastrous ownership of Ted Stepien, who makes the Haslams look like the geniuses. Michael Jordan derailed the resurgence in the late 1980s before hitting another dark period that was only interrupted by LeBron James. (Perhaps not a name to be bringing up this weekend.) The Indians were a “3,000 fans on a weeknight game” for all of the 1970s and 1980s, but have evolved into the town’s gold standard, despite having the longest current drought without a World Series title in Major League Baseball at 77 years and counting. But this is a Browns site, so let’s get back to the question at hand. We would never want to discourage someone from joining the family, so what advice would we give someone thinking of signing up for this? Try your best to enjoy those three hours on a Sunday afternoon and don’t let the losing, the sometimes comical play, the things you see that you can never unsee, get you down. Go with the flow, cheer, but understand that, for now, things are going to remain bad. And try to get to a game before the team moves into its new indoor stadium in 2029. The new stadium will be nicer, but the tailgating experience will likely not be the same. But the good news is, with a young core built off the past two drafts, and the prospect (as always) of the next franchise quarterback being just one draft away, the Browns may be nearing the end of the beginning of this current rebuild. If you think about it that way, this could be one of those opportunities where you can buy low as a fan, suffer for maybe a year or two, then get to reap the rewards as the team finally figures out how to stop losing games and learns to start winning them. OK, enough from me. Time for everyone else to have their say. What advice would you give Mr. Sparrow or anyone else thinking of booking a seat on the Browns bandwagon? Let us know in the comments.

title: 3 under-the-radar battles during Browns training camp
summary: It’s time! Cleveland Browns training camp. The rookies have reported, and next Tuesday, July 28, the veteran players will report. No more excursions to the local Chinese buffet. No more homemade key lime pie from the local bakery or grocery store. No more telling the team nutritionist that they were sure that crab legs and […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 03: Donovan McMillon #31 of the Cleveland Browns runs a drill during the Cleveland Browns OTA Offseason Workouts at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 03, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images It’s time! Cleveland Browns training camp. The rookies have reported, and next Tuesday, July 28, the veteran players will report. No more excursions to the local Chinese buffet. No more homemade key lime pie from the local bakery or grocery store. No more telling the team nutritionist that they were sure that crab legs and fried wings from Popeye’s were on their dietary plan. RELATED: INJURY LINGERS HEADING INTO 2026 TRAINING CAMP The running is about to begin. Eventually, the pads will go on, and the hitting will become the norm. Right now, it is 90 players in camp. Before Week 1, that number will become 53 players with 16 on the practice squad, plus one more guy as an international prospect. These weeks in camp will determine who will start, who will become the backups, and who will be sent along their way. Quite a few positional battles every single day. Here are three that most folks aren’t talking about. QB Dillon Gabriel vs. QB Taylen Green The biggest headline during this year’s training camp is Deshaun Watson against Shedeur Sanders for who will be the starting quarterback in 2026. But the QB3 slot will eventually be ironed out as well. Some say that Gabriel should somehow slide in between Watson and Sanders and be a candidate for the starting job, but most likely, he will receive very few first-team reps. The coaching staff has full attention on both Watson and Sanders for the Week 1 starter, with the loser listed as the backup. Gabriel (5’-11”, 205 pounds) started six games for the Browns in his rookie season and went 1-5-0. He tossed 185 passes with 110 completions for 937 yards and a 59.5% completion ratio. He was able to connect on 45 first-down conversions with seven TD passes and only two interceptions. As a runner, Gabriel had 14 attempts for 86 yards, converted four first-down conversions, and did not score. His competitor in camp will be rookie Taylen Green from Arkansas. Right off, Green’s 6’6” height is a huge asset for an NFL quarterback, but he is a lean 227 pounds. He runs like a gazelle and simply glides. Very shifty runner, plenty of juke moves, and can move the team down the field with his legs. In his senior year alone, Green had 777 rushing yards. That number is the envy of plenty of college running backs. For his college career, he had 459 carries. Marinate on that for a second. Almost 500 times rushing the ball – for a quarterback. He finished his college career with 2,405 rushing yards and scored 35 rushing touchdowns. An amazing athlete carrying the ball who was clocked at 4.36 and had a vertical jump of 43.5 inches. So, why was Green drafted in Round 6? Now for the gloomy news. He is a below-average passer. Rated 67% on his short passes. Average release speed because of an elongated throwing motion. His intermediate accuracy is horrible, especially when rushed. Green does not know when to leave the pocket or throw the ball away and live another down. And he is a turnover machine. He fumbled 18 times during his college years, plus had 35 interceptions. Now, he had huge career numbers: 9,662 passing yards, 198 completions on 326 attempts, a decent 60.1% completion ratio, and tossed 59 touchdowns while playing in 53 games. Both quarterbacks were invited and participated in the Senior Bowl. Gabriel left practice week as viewed the most NFL-ready quarterback. Green left game week displaying his accuracy skills may never be right. The fight for backup TE After a sterling rookie season, TE Harold Fannin appears to become a much more utilized component in newly-hired Todd Monken’s offense. He was a receiving machine while in college, and continued that trend when he hit the NFL. Monken’s offense will use quite a few multiple tight-end sets. 12 personnel will become a mainstay just like when he was the OC with the Baltimore Ravens. Most likely, Blake Whiteheart might cement that second tight end spot, although that isn’t a given. Monken used quite a bit of trey sets as well, where one tight end will line up like a fullback between the offensive line and the QB, while the other tight end is in the slot right beside a receiver, who is positioned outside – all on the same side. But 13 personnel will be on the field quite a bit as well. Monken wants to run the ball, and that takes blockers. Tight ends are simply extensions of the offensive line. There are plenty of candidates who will fight for the third tight end spot. The Browns should keep four TEs on the final roster and currently have six in camp. Jack Stoll (6’-4”, 247 pounds) Arguably, the best blocking tight end on the roster. This may give him the edge if the Browns’ running game is successful. He hasn’t been asked to catch many passes in his five seasons in the league. 41 targets with 28 receptions, nine first-down conversions, and one touchdown is nothing to write grandma about. But again, he is a blocker and excels at it. Joe Royer (6’-5”, 240 pounds) This rookie has been mentioned as a possible competitor for Whiteheart’s TE2 spot. He has great hands and has what it takes to become that second tight end Monken will need to run his offense. Royer has drawn Travis Kelce comparisons. This kid shows exceptional body control and spatial awareness. He can contort his body and catch poorly-thrown passes. He creates good separation on intermediate throws and will run angry after the catch. Royer also gives the offense good YAC numbers. Brenden Bates (6’-5”, 255 pounds) Bates is now the veteran presence in this group, having played two seasons. Like Stoll, he offers the offense simply one thing: blocking abilities. He has just six targets with four catches for 48 yards, and is a reliable blocker. Carsen Ryan (6’-3”, 255 pounds) This is the Wild Card in the group. If Ryan comes into camp and shows his excellent pass-catching abilities , he could see a lot of TE3 looks or even become the receiving pairing with Fannin in 12 personnel groupings. He is a sixth-round draft pick for a reason. Excellent versatility and his work ethic is unmatched. High character. He finished with a 75.3 Pro Football Focus run-blocking grade in 2025. Ryan offers discipline, toughness, and balance. He reflects persistence, adaptability, and a deep football foundation. He offers versatility in that he can play in-line, off the line of scrimmage, run blocking, and has receiving abilities. Very competitive with high energy. Browns fans will love this kid, but he needs to show out early and often. S Donovan McMillon vs. S Daniel Thomas Typically, the Browns only keep four safeties , although one year they kept five when Joe Woods was the defensive coordinator and utilized the 4-2-5 consistently. He inserted a safety for one of the linebackers. Obviously, SS Grant Delpit and FS Ronnie Hickman are the starting safeties this year. But behind them are several guys who will be called upon for lots of playing time. Rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren was taken in Round 2 and will solidify that third position. But who will man the fourth spot? Currently, Cleveland has seven safeties in camp: Donovan McMillan, Daniel Thomas, Zion Washington, and Chris Edmonds. Our money is on a McMillon-Thomas bout. Whoever wins this will earn that fourth roster spot, play quite a bit on special teams in punt/kickoff coverage, and earn plenty of defensive reps. Thomas (5’-10”, 215 pounds) entered the league in 2020 as a fifth-round pick of the Jacksonville Jaguars. He signed with Cleveland during this year’s free agency period and was given a two-year deal worth $3 million. This means he expects to stay a while. He has played in 83 NFL games with 94 career tackles, 0 sacks, 1 tackle for loss, 1 fumble recovery, 1 interception, 3 batted passes, 0 pressures,…

title: Realistic, unrealistic Browns expectations for this upcoming season
summary: As the summer winds down, training camp for all 32 teams will begin towards the end of July. For the Cleveland Browns, the team will go into Year 2 of their rebuild. Star defensive end Myles Garrett is in Inglewood, former head coach Kevin Stefanski is in Atlanta, and the team has a new head […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 10: Head coach Todd Monken of the Cleveland Browns reacts during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 10, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the summer winds down, training camp for all 32 teams will begin towards the end of July. For the Cleveland Browns, the team will go into Year 2 of their rebuild. Star defensive end Myles Garrett is in Inglewood , former head coach Kevin Stefanski is in Atlanta , and the team has a new head coach in Todd Monken. Current sportsbooks have the Browns over/under for wins at 5.5 . A young offense and defense with an unproven head coach. A team filled with questions and not a lot of answers. Unrealistic Expectation: The Browns contending for a playoff spot Before Cleveland traded Garrett, it wouldn’t be out of the equation for the Browns to contend for a wild card spot in the AFC. A young offense with explosive playmakers, a defense that had Garrett, and an easy schedule would have some fans thinking Cleveland could surprise everyone. Unfortunately, it’s not the case. Looking at the landscape of the AFC, the Browns are nowhere close to contending for a playoff spot. The team has too many unknowns on both sides of the ball. Offense is young with playmakers but uncertainty at the QB position Defense has young talent but lacks a true alpha on the team HC is a question mark due to his inexperience as a head coach. Realistic Expectation: Offense will struggle for the 1st half of the season Installing a new offense might seem easy, but it’s more of a steep learning curve. Learning the new terminology in terms of the playbook, and an entire offensive line being revamped, creates a lot of questions. Expecting the offense to have fireworks from the start is an unrealistic expectation. Monken will bring over what he did with the Baltimore Ravens to the Cleveland Browns. Heavy usage of play-action with an emphasis on the run game. The passing game will be a work in progress, but the running game will determine the ceiling of this offense and how good it will be towards the second half of the season. The offense will struggle for the first 6 weeks of the season before finding a form of consistency towards the second half of the season. Realistic Expectation: The team will be picking towards the top 10, not top 3 of the NFL Draft On paper, the Browns aren’t as bad as they were going into last season. Offensively, the offensive line and receivers look better on paper, but the quarterback position is still a question mark. Defensively, trading Garrett was a huge blow. However, the team still has young, talented pieces in defensive tackle Mason Graham, Linebacker/Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger, and defensive end Jared Verse. Realistically, the team can be competitive but not bad enough that they will be picking towards the top two. Combine that with a fairly easy schedule, and the team could win more than four games and be out of the running for a top three pick What are your realistic and unrealistic expectations for the Browns season? title: Cowboys news: Things to look for at training camp
summary: Cowboys to Oxnard 2026: What to watch for at training camp – Cody Warren, Inside the Star Pay attention to these storylines when the Cowboys open camp. Cowboys training camp starts July 28th in Oxnard, California, and I’m ready for the guessing and speculation about players and positions to start. We’ve spent the entire offseason thinking […]
full_text: OXNARD, CA - AUGUST 05: Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer slaps hands with his players during the Los Angeles Rams - Dallas Cowboys joint Training Camp on August 05, 2025, at the River Ridge Playing Fields in Oxnard, CA. (Photo by Jevone Moore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Cowboys to Oxnard 2026: What to watch for at training camp – Cody Warren, Inside the Star Pay attention to these storylines when the Cowboys open camp. Cowboys training camp starts July 28th in Oxnard, California , and I’m ready for the guessing and speculation about players and positions to start. We’ve spent the entire offseason thinking about what we think the roster will look like, what players will start, who will break out this season, and what will a Christian Parker defense actually look like. Everything up to this point is just talk until the pads come on. I don’t want everyone to lose their minds over every practice clip, either. Someone will catch an amazing pass over a practice squad player or camp body and start thinking that player is the second coming of Jerry Rice. Let’s pump the brakes right now. There are bigger storylines to watch. Will DeMarvion Overshown and Shavon Revel Jr. Look Like Themselves at Training Camp? I haven’t heard anything to make me think these two will not be ready for training camp. Overshown’s game depends on speed , reaction, and playing without hesitation. Will he be thinking about his knee while trying to chase down offensive players? We will know pretty quick. I’ll be watching how quickly he closes, how his change of direction is, and how he responds after getting a few physical practices in. Shavon Revel Jr. has similar issues, just at a different position. We know a cornerback cannot play scared. I want to see how Revel plants his foot, turns, runs, and if he trusts his body with a receiver coming out of a break. If we see an aggressive Revel in press coverage and fighting with receivers, that will tell me more than a practice report. As a Cowboys fan and watching what this defense went through last season, two great players don’t just need to be available, I want to see them being explosive. The Running Back Two Job Is Wide Open at Training Camp Javonte Williams enters training camp as the unrivaled number one back and that was solidified with statements from Will McClay . Even without Will McClay’s comment, I don’t think anyone was going to argue who the lead dog is. The real battle will be behind him. As we all know, and I have heavily talked about in the past, Jaydon Blue has speed on top of speed. This guy has the attributes to be the home run hitter on the ground. Blue’s biggest issue last season was maturity and I think that has been fixed. Phil Mafah is the opposite of Blue. He’s big, real big, and plays with force and a blatant disregard for defensive players safety and I like it. This could be the guy who helps solve our red zone woes. Malik Davis came on strong at the end of the season and should not be counted out. Yes, he has bounced around on a few teams, but seemed to put it all together at the end of 2025. He’s not great at anything, but seemed to be good at just about everything. Sounds like a RB2. The two other running backs headed into training camp are Israel Abanikanda and rookie Dominic Richardson. Israel is a player the Cowboys liked coming out of the University of Pittsburgh in 2023. He is a speedy back who broke Tony Dorsett’s single-game rushing record while at Pitt. The best Dallas Cowboys player to wear No. 19 might surprise some people – Luke Norris, The Landry Hat What do you guys think? Do you agree this is the best player in Cowboys history to wear number 19? Welcome back to The Landry Hat’s series covering the best Dallas Cowboys players to wear every jersey number from No. 0 to No. 99 . Well, we’ve officially reached the one-fifth mark of our journey, as we’ve come to our 20th entry, and we’ve got a nice little battle here for the No. 19 slot. So, without further ado, let’s take a quick look at everyone who’s donned the digit for America’s Team over the years. Lance Alworth, WR Miles Austin, WR Brice Butler, WR Amari Cooper, WR Ryan Flournoy, WR Noah Igbinoghene, CB John Jett, P Keyshawn Johnson, WR Trey Lance, QB Clint Longley, QB Brett Maher, K Lance Rentzel, WR Kevin Sweeney, QB From an overall historical perspective, the most notable name on this list is Lance Alworth, who’s the only player listed above to be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. But as he made his name with the San Diego Chargers and only played a pair of seasons with the Cowboys, he’s out, although it should be noted that he won a ring in the first of those two campaigns, catching 34 passes for 487 yards with a pair of touchdowns in 1971. Going back to that same era, Lance Rentzel had a solid four-year run with Dallas from 1967 to 1970, catching 183 passes for 3,521 yards with 31 touchdowns. But he’s on the outside looking in as well. When all was said and done, though, this became a two-man race between players who suited up in this century. Now, many might go with Amari Cooper in this slot. And he’s certainly got a strong case, as he had a strong three-and-a-half-year run in Big D, catching 292 passes for 3,893 yards with 27 touchdowns and earning a pair of Pro Bowl selections. But our call here is Miles Austin, which might surprise some people. But it might also surprise some to know (or remember) that he also made a pair of Pro Bowls and that his best season was better than any that Cooper had during his entire career. Throw in the fact that he also returned kicks, and his value was just higher. 8 offense vs. defense training camp battles to watch-Mike Poland, Blogging the Boys As things heat up, keep a close eye on these hotly contested battles. Training camp is where roster battles are decided, but some of the most interesting work in Oxnard come from players competing on opposite sides of the football. The Cowboys have a strong mix of established stars and young players looking to break out, which should create plenty of entertaining one-on-one matchups. These battles will not determine starting jobs on their own, but tell us a lot about which players are improving, who may be ready for a bigger role and where Dallas could still have concerns entering the season. Here are eight matchups Cowboys fans should be watching closely throughout training camp this year. 8. Anthony Smith vs. Devin Moore This rookie-on-rookie matchup could affect the back end of two unsettled position groups. Smith’s size and vertical speed will test Moore’s ability to turn and run, while Moore’s length should challenge Smith to beat press coverage and win contested catches. 7. Drew Shelton vs. L.T. Overton Two fourth-round rookies will have plenty to prove when the pads come on. Shelton’s athleticism will test Overton’s ability to push the edge, while Overton’s power and versatility should provide an early examination of Shelton’s technique and anchor. 6. title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: DB Zion Childress
summary: Zion Childress did a lot to increase his stock in last year’s training camp and hopes to take it even further in 2026 with a roster spot. He’ll need to impress a new defensive coaching staff to do it, and perhaps show his value at a new position in the Cowboys’ secondary. Background Years in […]
full_text: Zion Childress did a lot to increase his stock in last year’s training camp and hopes to take it even further in 2026 with a roster spot. He’ll need to impress a new defensive coaching staff to do it, and perhaps show his value at a new position in the Cowboys’ secondary. Background Years in NFL: 1 Acquired by: UDFA (2025) Childress came out of Kentucky last year with exceptional versatility, reportedly having played every possible role at both cornerback and safety during his collegiate career. Perhaps the proverbial “Jack of all trades, master of none” label, along with noted issues in his tackling ability, caused him to go undrafted. He was quickly signed by the Cowboys as a free agent. Working mostly as a slot corner, Childress was consistently praised throughout the offseason. Though it wasn’t enough to get him onto the 53-man roster, Childress did make the practice squad and was called up for the first two regular-season games for special teams duties. Ahead of Week 3, the Houston Texans poached Childress away from Dallas. He did not appear in a game for them and was waived about a month later. The Cowboys hadn’t lost track of Childress, signing him back to the practice squad just a couple of days later. He got called up for one more game last year in November, and finally got a few snaps on defense. That January, he signed a new deal to return with Dallas in 2026. Contract Status Years Left: 2 2026 Cap Hit: $1.01 million As often happens with guys signed from the practice squad, Childress essentially got a new version of his original UDFA contract. It’s still for minimal money and runs through his projected third season, when he would then be a restricted free agent in 2028. 2026 Projections Role: Backup DB Roster Chance: 10% Though he’s still listed as a CB on the Cowboys’ official roster, reports from the spring camps had Childress taking all of his reps at safety. This may indicate a position switch is in the works, or just that Dallas has seen enough of his corner work and now wanted to evaluate his versatility. With Christian Parker’s arrival as defensive coordinator, there’s a new emphasis on safeties who can also drop down and defend the slot. That ability was highlighted in the free agent signings of Jalen Thompson and P.J. Locke, and is now the plan for rookie Caleb Downs. If this is the new blueprint for what Dallas wants in its safeties, or at least some of them, Childress seems a good fit. However, you can’t play safety if you can’t tackle. This knock on Childress’ game from his college days may already be rectified, but it’s worth monitoring as he tries to force his way onto the 53. Even if veterans Malik Hooker and Markquese Bell are being phased out in Dallas, core skills and experience won’t be easily overcome by Childress or other developing prospects. The Cowboys are likely facing some tough decisions in their secondary at final cuts. Alijah Clark is another DB prospect with versatility and perhaps an emerging lead role on special teams. There are a slew of intriguing cornerbacks like Caelen Carson, Josh Butler, Reddy Steward, Derion Kendrick, and Trikweze Bridges who are all battling for the last spot or two on that depth chart. A few guys are going to have great camps but still get pinched by the numbers, and Childress could easily be among them. Like the rest of the competition, all Childress can do now is perform. If he can at least maintain last year’s momentum, it should get him back to the practice squad. For anything more, he’ll need to shine on special teams and earn trust for expanded defensive duties. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 50
summary: It is Day 50 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Dec 15, 2013; Arlington, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys defensive end DeMarcus Ware (94) with his helmet off during a timeout from the game against the Green Bay Packers at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Emmons-Imagn Images It is Day 50 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. We’re now at the halfway point, Day 50. of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, so let’s make this one special and revisit a game that combined a comfortable Cowboys win with a major franchise milestone. Dallas hosted the St. Louis Rams in Week 3 of the 2013 season needing a bounce-back performance after a road loss to Kansas City. The Cowboys got exactly that behind DeMarco Murray’s rushing, Tony Romo’s efficiency, and a defensive front that overwhelmed Sam Bradford all afternoon. But this game also became the moment a franchise record was set. Sunday, September 22, 2013 — 1:00 p.m. ET AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 31, St. Louis Rams 7 The tone was set early. Dallas opened with a strong Murray-led drive, and Romo finished it with a two-yard touchdown pass to Dez Bryant. Dan Bailey added a short field goal later in the first quarter, and the Cowboys led 10-0 after holding St. Louis to only two total yards in the opening period. That was the shape of the game from the start. The Cowboys kept building in the second quarter. Murray continued to punish St. Louis on the ground, and Dallas put together a 10-play, 67-yard drive that ended with Murray diving to the pylon for a touchdown. By halftime, the Cowboys led 17-0 and had turned the game into exactly the kind of physical, low-stress afternoon Jason Garrett’s team needed. The third quarter brought more of the same. Murray ripped off a 41-yard run early in the half, setting up Romo’s 24-yard touchdown pass to rookie tight end Gavin Escobar. The Rams finally got on the board when Bradford found Austin Pettis for a touchdown, but that was their only real scoring threat of the day. Dallas answered in the fourth quarter when Romo hit Dwayne Harris for a 24-yard touchdown, closing out the 31-7 rout. Murray was the offensive star, rushing 26 times for 175 yards and a touchdown. Romo did not need volume to control the game, finishing with 210 passing yards and three touchdown throws to three different receivers. Jason Witten led Dallas with five catches for 67 yards, while the Cowboys’ offense finished with 396 total yards and controlled the game from the first drive. But the lasting headline belonged to DeMarcus Ware. Ware had two sacks, giving him 115 for his Cowboys career and moving him past Harvey Martin for the most sacks in franchise history. His first sack tied Martin’s mark, and his second put the record in Ware’s hands alone. For one of the greatest defensive players the franchise has ever had, it was a fitting record-setting performance. This game belongs on the countdown because franchise records matter, especially when they involve a player like Ware passing a legend like Harvey Martin. The Cowboys have had elite defenders across generations, from Martin and Randy White to Charles Haley, Ware, and Micah Parsons. On this day, Ware officially climbed to the top of the sack list, while Dallas turned the Rams into a footnote on a milestone afternoon. So for this halfway point of the countdown, we dedicate it to great and powerful Demarcus Ware. Who remembers when @DeMarcusWare became the All-Time sack leader for @dallascowboys in 2013? It was a sack feast against the Rams, but Ware finally took the crown in a 2 sack game, overtaking Randy White and Harvey Martin! What a time to be alive! #Dallascowboys #Cowboys #NFL … pic.twitter.com/ZXNgaMNNod — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 24, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Ware finished with two sacks, six tackles, and two additional quarterback hits. His second sack gave him 115 career sacks, passing Martin for the franchise record, where that record still stands today. title: 3 reasons why the Dallas Cowboys should sign LB Bobby Wagner
summary: Any hopes of the Dallas Cowboys trading for Jordyn Brooks to upgrade their linebacker position have now gone out the window after the Miami Dolphins signed him to a three-year, $51.3 million contract extension earlier this week. With that no longer an option, they should now set their sights on free agent LB Bobby Wagner. […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - DECEMBER 7: Bobby Wagner #54 of the Washington Commanders looks on during an NFL football game against the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium on December 07, 2025 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Any hopes of the Dallas Cowboys trading for Jordyn Brooks to upgrade their linebacker position have now gone out the window after the Miami Dolphins signed him to a three-year, $51.3 million contract extension earlier this week. With that no longer an option, they should now set their sights on free agent LB Bobby Wagner. Below are three reasons why. Reason #1: Talent upgrade Even at 36 years old, Bobby Wagner would immediately upgrade the position. He may not be the player he once was, but is still playing as one of the best off-ball LBs in the league. He earned an overall 78.6 PFF defensive grade, ninth among 88 qualified players at the position. His run-defense grade (93.3) ranked fifth and his pass-rush grade (92.4) ranked second. He did struggle in coverage, ranking 51 st in the league with a 51.1 grade. Reason #2: Experience/leadership Wagner has proven to be an ironman throughout his career, starting at least 15 games each season since 2015 and all 17 in the last two years. The Cowboys don’t currently have anyone even close with that kind of starting experience; the closest is Dee Winters with 27 career starts. With all of his years of accumulated knowledge/experience, Wagner could be the leader this position is currently lacking and serve as a mentor both on and off the field to Dallas’ young LBs. Reason #3: Insurance policy DeMarvion Overshown and Dee Winters are the Cowboys projected starters entering training camp, with this year’s third-round pick Jaishawn Barham a close third on the depth chart. After that Dallas’ potential candidates to start are few and far between. By signing Wagner, that all changes. Not only do they get a future Hall of Famer still playing at a high level, but someone capable of being a full-time starter if Overshown doesn’t work out as planned. Would you sign Wagner? Hit the comments and let us know.

title: One prediction for training camp, wide receivers edition
summary: We continue our Dallas Cowboys training camp prediction series, and today we land on one of the most explosive, deep and capable position groups of any team in the NFL – the wide receivers. Of course, Cowboys fans understand just how good this position group was last year and that there is still potential for […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 16: Marquise Robinson #28 of the Baltimore Ravens defends a pass intended for Jonathan Mingo #81 of the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter of an NFL Preseason 2025 game at AT&T Stadium on August 16, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images We continue our Dallas Cowboys training camp prediction series, and today we land on one of the most explosive, deep and capable position groups of any team in the NFL – the wide receivers. Of course, Cowboys fans understand just how good this position group was last year and that there is still potential for growth. Although most of the series thus far has been about who will step up, for this position group, which is deep and full of playmakers, the reality is that some guys just won’t be good enough to make the cut. Unfortunately for Jonathan Mingo, he will likely be on the way out once camp and the preseason conclude. Prediction: Jonathan Mingo will not make the roster Mingo is currently sitting in the same spot as fellow receivers KaVontae Turpin and Marquez Valdes-Scantling, which is beyond the top three receivers – CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and Ryan Flournoy. Now, obviously, part of this prediction must consider how many WRs Dallas is going to carry into the season, but even if the Cowboys decide to carry six or more receivers, Mingo’s path onto the roster is difficult. Positionally, ahead of him are Turpin and Valdes-Scantling, both of whom have something Mingo does not: a touchdown in the NFL. That, along with Turpin’s ability in the return game and Valdes-Scantling’s contributions over his soon-to-be nine-year career, puts Mingo in an uphill battle. At the same time, Mingo is trending in the wrong direction in virtually every statistical category. Since his rookie season, the number of targets, receptions and yards have declined every single year. Last year he played in six games and caught one pass for 25 yards. Mingo, however, is the youngest of the receivers mentioned, and his physical ability will give him a shot to crack the 53-man roster, but if the Cowboys decide to carry only five receivers this year, it will be an uphill battle for the 25-year-old receiver. Will Mingo make it? Who do you have down as the Cowboys WRs coming out of camp?
