title: Players who are being overshadowed by a great Cowboys offseason
summary: Before we know it, the Dallas Cowboys will touch down in Oxnard, CA. Every summer, storylines will rule the news cycle with several questions to be answered. Who are the players that are fighting for roster spots? Who will win their position battle? Who is the player that no one saw coming? The Cowboys aren’t […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys linebacker Shemar James (50) goes through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images Before we know it, the Dallas Cowboys will touch down in Oxnard, CA. Every summer, storylines will rule the news cycle with several questions to be answered. Who are the players that are fighting for roster spots? Who will win their position battle? Who is the player that no one saw coming? The Cowboys aren’t ever short of conversation when it comes to dissecting the team, especially not this season when it comes to topics like George Pickens. Yet, the other question one must ask: Who is getting lost in the shuffle? What players are being forgotten? Here are four players that aren’t being talked about enough ahead of training camp. Jalen Thompson While the Dallas Cowboys and their fans are rightfully thrilled to have Caleb Downs, it somehow almost makes you forget that the Cowboys picked up a pretty good safety in Jalen Thompson. Thompson, along with Downs and Malik Hooker, gives Dallas a deep safety room that affords them the luxury of playing a different array of coverages. While some may attribute that to Downs, Thompson also plays a big part. He can play two deep coverage, he can play down in the box and play some slot in a pinch. He has averaged 100 tackles per season over the last five years. With all the news and storylines surrounding the team, you don’t hear much about Thompson. Expect Thompson to have a terrific season and be a very dependable player despite the lack of fanfare. Marquez Valdes-Scantling Dallas has a top-heavy wide receiver room that boasts CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens as the “Star” attractions. Furthermore, Pickens’ contract status occupies a lot of the conversation when it comes to Dallas’ receivers. Plus, behind Lamb and Pickens is Ryan Flournoy, who showed flashes last season with multiple 100-yard games. A breakout for Ryan Flournoy feels almost imminent given the Cowboys’ offense with Dak Prescott at the controls. Meanwhile, the excitement around newcomers Anthony Smith and Denzel Mims has fans thinking Smith may pay immediate dividends as a speedy big target with enticing upside, and a potential career-resurgence story for Mims. This allows Marquez Valdes-Scantling to quietly fly under the radar. Valdes-Scantling has had a pretty respectable career as a complementary receiver. He has won two championships with the Kansas City Chiefs and is a certified deep threat. He has averaged 16.8 yards per reception for his career and has an average depth of target of 15.7 yards beyond the line of scrimmage. He has to make the roster first, but there just may be a surprise player there that many people have already dismissed. Nick Leverett Backup center is now one of the positions to keep an eye on moving forward this season. At first, the Cowboys secured a very good backup behind Cooper Beebe with the signing of Matt Hennessy. Unfortunately, Hennessy was placed on season-ending injured reserve with a neck injury, elevating the need for a reliable option. T.J. Bass is expected to work into the mix, but well-traveled veteran Nick Leverett is penciled in as Beebe’s backup. As the summer picks up, it’ll be interesting to see how Leverett fares. You can already expect that he will get a large workload in the preseason matchups. If Leverett can hold his own, he could, at worst, secure a safe place on the roster and, at best, the number two job behind Beebe. Leverett has largely gone unnoticed because, let’s face it, we wouldn’t need to familiarize ourselves with him unless something went wrong. As for the team, Dallas likely would prefer that Leverett would be able to hold down the fort in Beebe’s absence so Bass is available to fill in at either guard spot if needed. Shemar James With the complete makeover that the Cowboys defense has undergone, it caused many to completely move past an abysmal 2025 defense, and the anticipation of a better unit has caused some players that were on last year’s defense to recede into the background. One person in particular is Shemar James. James had a lot of time on the field as a rookie and, by the bare numbers, put up some good stats. However, what that also showed was a player that was being heavily counted on and appeared to be overwhelmed at times. James was one of the youngest players in the draft as he was only 20 years old when he was selected by the Cowboys, and it showed as he had his challenges with adjusting to a full workload in the NFL. The hope is the will improve exponentially under a technician such as Christian Parker. Why he has faded into the crowd somewhat is because of the expectations on DeMarvion Overshown, and Dallas acquiring Dee Winters by trade during the draft. Still, there’s a lot to like about James’ game. He has terrific speed to play laterally and has great closing speed coming downhill. Also, James has already seen some time with the first-team unit this offseason, so he isn’t far behind from making a relatively significant impact even if he is being talked about much.

title: 8 offense vs. defense training camp battles to watch
summary: Training camp is where roster battles are decided, but some of the most interesting work in Oxnard come from players competing on opposite sides of the football. The Cowboys have a strong mix of established stars and young players looking to break out, which should create plenty of entertaining one-on-one matchups. These battles will not […]
full_text: Training camp is where roster battles are decided, but some of the most interesting work in Oxnard come from players competing on opposite sides of the football. The Cowboys have a strong mix of established stars and young players looking to break out, which should create plenty of entertaining one-on-one matchups. These battles will not determine starting jobs on their own, but tell us a lot about which players are improving, who may be ready for a bigger role and where Dallas could still have concerns entering the season. Here are eight matchups Cowboys fans should be watching closely throughout training camp this year. 8. Anthony Smith vs. Devin Moore This rookie-on-rookie matchup could affect the back end of two unsettled position groups. Smith’s size and vertical speed will test Moore’s ability to turn and run, while Moore’s length should challenge Smith to beat press coverage and win contested catches. 7. Drew Shelton vs. L.T. Overton Two fourth-round rookies will have plenty to prove when the pads come on. Shelton’s athleticism will test Overton’s ability to push the edge, while Overton’s power and versatility should provide an early examination of Shelton’s technique and anchor. 6. Brevyn Spann-Ford vs. Jalen Thompson Spann-Ford has an opportunity to overtake Luke Schoonmaker and establish himself as the Cowboys’ second tight end. His size will create problems at the catch point, but Thompson’s experience, instincts and physicality should provide a difficult test in both coverage and the running game. 5. Jaydon Blue vs. Jaishawn Barham This should be one of the most athletic battles in camp. Blue’s speed will test Barham’s pursuit angles and open-field tackling, while Barham can challenge the running back’s pass protection when he is used as a blitzer. 4. Ryan Flournoy vs. DaRon Bland Flournoy is trying to maintain his role as the third receiver after showing progress last season. Facing an instinctive ballhawk such as Bland will force him to sharpen his routes and consistently create separation. Bland will also use the matchup to prove he is healthy and ready to reclaim his place as Dallas’ top cornerback. 3. Terence Steele vs. Donovan Ezeiruaku Steele remains one of the biggest concerns on the offensive line, while Ezeiruaku is looking to make a second-year jump. Ezeiruaku’s speed and bend should test Steele’s footwork, while Steele’s strength will reveal whether the young pass rusher can handle the physical demands of playing every down. 2. CeeDee Lamb vs. Caleb Downs There may not be a better learning opportunity for Downs than covering Lamb from the slot. Lamb’s releases, route running and understanding of leverage will punish mistakes, but those daily repetitions could accelerate the rookie’s development and prepare him for a major role in the secondary. 1. George Pickens vs. Shavon Revel Jr. Pickens against Revel could be the most entertaining matchup of training camp. Pickens is a physical receiver who excels at the catch point, making him the perfect test for Revel’s technique, confidence and ball skills. With Revel another year removed from his ACL injury, this battle should show how far the young cornerback has developed.

title: Cowboys news: Dallas is benefiting from quiet offseason
summary: Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things – Todd Archer, ESPN This is exactly what the Cowboys needed. “There won’t be negotiations on a long-term deal,” Stephen Jones said. It was another perfect only with the Cowboys moment where contract negotiations have become a never-ending story. In 2023, All-Pro right guard Zack Martin held out […]
full_text: Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things – Todd Archer, ESPN This is exactly what the Cowboys needed. “There won’t be negotiations on a long-term deal,” Stephen Jones said. It was another perfect only with the Cowboys moment where contract negotiations have become a never-ending story. In 2023, All-Pro right guard Zack Martin held out of a portion of training camp looking to renegotiate his contract. In 2024, the talks surrounded the futures of Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb with the Pro Bowl wide receiver missing most of training camp before an extension was reached. Prescott’s record $60 million annual deal would be agreed to on the morning of the season opener. And then last year, the mess that surrounded Micah Parsons ‘ contract saga that eventually saw the All-Pro pass rusher traded to the Green Bay Packers a week before the 2025 season started. It all pointed to more drama in 2026. But Pickens, who will make $27.3 million on the tag, attended the mandatory minicamp in June and said he will not hold out of training camp. July 15, the deadline for Pickens to sign a long-term extension, came and went with barely a note . It was like a balloon that flitters away when the air is released. The potential of drama was gone. Dallas Cowboys Training Camp Primer: Five biggest storylines heading into Oxnard – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram Things to keep an eye on. New line of defense It’s a new year, and it’s a brand-new defense under new coordinator Christian Parker . And while there is quite a bit we can pull from his press availabilities about how much the unit will see change, it’s tough to truly envision it until it hits the field. How has he solved the communication problems that plagued the unit last season? How will the 3-4 scheme find consistent pressure? Who will hold the bulk of the responsibilities in the secondary? Those questions might not get full answers in Oxnard, but the on-field product that we will see will offer a ton of insight into the unit that Parker has constructed over the past six months. Personnel-wise, there are a lot of new faces with things to prove. Rashan Gary was traded from the only NFL team he’s known (Green Bay) in April. Jalen Thompson arrives with the biggest free agent contract in team history. Caleb Downs walks into the NFL with sky-high expectations , and fellow first-round pick Malachi Lawrence will be looked at for a premium role as well. After poor linebacker play in 2025, Dee Winters is back in DFW to see if he can be the solution in the middle . The expectations remain the same on offense. On defense, the level of play has to take a significant step forward. How far has it come? We’ll at least get a head start on answering that question in the next month. 2) Is Dak Prescott a legitimate MVP candidate for 2026? Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com Will Dak Prescott have himself in the MVP conversation this season? Patrik : It tickles me to see some people act as if this question is bold or unreasonable (I call that the “Cowboy Tax”) when, in actuality, it’s so reasonable that it almost earns a yawn from me. Let’s talk facts here, or science, if you will. Prescott is an All-Pro quarterback that has been at the front of the NFL MVP conversation not once or twice, but three times over the last five seasons — to the point where there’s a contingent that argues he should’ve won the honor over Lamar Jackson in 2023. So, can Prescott be a legitimate MVP candidate again when the 2026 season rolls around? Yes, and yes again. He’s at the top of his game. He’s got weapons galore. He’s got an offensive play-caller that invites fresh ideas and proved he can call a No. 1 offense. If the Cowboys’ defense plays up to expectation under Christian Parker, or at least above average, Prescott’s play won’t be wasted with a playoff-less campaign or early postseason exit and, then and only then, will the world be willing to give the former fourth-round pick his credit … following a playoff run that requires both sides of the team to show up every week and not just Prescott and the offense. (*yawns*) Former Cowboys QB Will Grier to join Dallas staff as assistant coach – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News Will Grier is back in Dallas. Former Dallas Cowboys and recently retired quarterback Will Grier will join the team as an offensive assistant coach, a person familiar with the move confirmed to The Dallas Morning News . Grier had briefly re-signed with the Carolina Panthers this offseason before ultimately deciding to retire earlier this month. The Cowboys actually had interest in adding Grier to the coaching staff this offseason before he signed with the Panthers. The offer, it appears, still stood. The 31-year-old spent the entirety of last season on the Cowboys practice squad , his second stint with the team. Tony Romo arrested on suspicion of intoxicated driving in Milwaukee – Saad Yousuf and Andrew Marchand, The Athletic The former Cowboys’ quarterback found touble. Lead NFL on CBS analyst and former Dallas Cowboys quarterback Tony Romo was arrested on suspicion of operating while intoxicated (OWI) Thursday evening, according to the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office. Romo was driving southbound on Interstate 43 in Milwaukee when he was pulled over. The arrest report obtained by The Athletic states that Romo performed poorly on the standardized field sobriety tests and was taken into custody as a result. Romo was released shortly after being booked and given a court date of Sept. 21. According to the Wisconsin Department of Transportation, a first-offense OWI carries a penalty of $150-$300, plus a $435 OWI surcharge. An OWI is Wisconsin’s equivalent to what other states call a DUI (driving under the influence) or DWI (driving while intoxicated). Daily discussion question: How will you spend the last weekend without Cowboys things going on?

title: All eyes are on Bo Nix as Broncos QB returns to the field
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! For the first time since January, Bo Nix will be a full go on a football field. With the Denver Broncos training camp set to start in a few days, it’s the first time Nix will be a full-go since the infamous gut punch. Not that anyone needs a reminder, but […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - JANUARY 17: Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix (10) waits for the snap in the third quarter against the Buffalo Bills in the AFC Divisional Round game at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! For the first time since January, Bo Nix will be a full go on a football field. With the Denver Broncos training camp set to start in a few days, it’s the first time Nix will be a full-go since the infamous gut punch. Not that anyone needs a reminder, but the Broncos had just recorded one of the best wins in franchise history after beating Josh Allen and the favored Buffalo Bills 33-30 in overtime. Broncos Country was giddy and in an absolute party mood. It was 30 minutes later that the news of Nix breaking his ankle hit, and the vibe swung to despair. All eyes will be on Nix when he steps foot on the practice field and will remain on him through the rest of training camp and the preseason. No amount of words will fight off the narrative battle and the questions of Nix’s ankle until people see. Still, Broncos head coach Sean Payton and Nix have done what they can to dispel those questions. Namely, that Nix will somehow be limited now, and he won’t have the same mobility because of the ankle injury. As Payton said to the media in the middle of June: “I think I mentioned this last week, and I think this is important. I don’t think when he’s fully recovered, and he’s out here participating (that) you’re going to see someone that doesn’t move. All of that, some of his superpowers, his ability to move and not get sacked, find throws — I don’t think any of that will be impacted at all. I think he’s working extremely hard on this recovery. I think he’s more than ahead of schedule.” Nix took the will he be the same QB and mobility question and flipped it on its head. “Well, my concern is they say it’s back healthy, as good as new, and I hadn’t really been like that in a couple years,” Nix said to the media in June, laughing. “So my concern is maybe moving around a little bit better.” This also isn’t the first time Nix has dealt with an ankle injury in his football life, so he knew what to do and how to approach it. “When I had an ankle injury in high school, we won the state championship,“ Nix said to the media. ”When I had an ankle injury in college, we went and won a lot of games at Oregon. Now I expect it to be the same thing. For me, it’s just another bump in the road. It’s another thing, but one thing I don’t necessarily worry about right now is my health. We play this game long enough, you get hurt, and you get bumps and bruises. We have great medicine nowadays and great training to where you get back on the field. “You look at some of the worst injuries you could get, and guys are playing the next year and feel stronger and better than ever. I think just where we are as a culture and a society, we just heal fast. We have a good operation of getting back healthy. I don’t worry about that at all. I think it probably won’t be the last time I’m injured and miss a couple games, but hopefully that’s not the case. Just take it however it comes and take it day-by-day. For right now, just getting back healthy and getting back to where once this season comes, it’s just right in the past for me, and I don’t even think about it.” Yes, all eyes will be on Nix as he steps on the football field as an active participant for the first time since his injury in January. What they see will be the quarterback who outdueled Allen for one of the best wins in Broncos’ history. And as Nix said, he may be even better.

title: Denver Broncos roster review: Safety Talanoa Hufanga
summary: The Denver Broncos have a storied history of safeties and cornerbacks donning the orange and blue. Whether it be via the draft or through free agency, the franchise has done well over the years finding players at both positions that compete at a high level on the backend of their defense. In the 2025 free […]
full_text: Sep 7, 2025; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos safety Talanoa Hufanga (9) after the game at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images The Denver Broncos have a storied history of safeties and cornerbacks donning the orange and blue. Whether it be via the draft or through free agency, the franchise has done well over the years finding players at both positions that compete at a high level on the backend of their defense. In the 2025 free agency period, one of the Broncos’ first big splashes was signing safety Talanoa Hufanga away from the San Francisco 49ers. A former All-Pro and Pro-Bowl player in 2022, Hufanga battled injuries in 2023 and 2024 that limited his impact and potential. Nevertheless, the former USC Standout earned a lucrative three-year deal with up to $45 million with $20 million in total guaranteed money. Hufanga’s first year in the Mile High City was productive. He stayed healthy for the entire season and started every game. Overall, he posted 106 tackles, 11 pass deflections, 1 forced fumble, and 2 sacks. Entering his second season with the Broncos, I’m a firm believer Hufanga will have an even larger impact for Denver in 2026. Let’s discuss. Talanoa Hufanga and Brandon Jones checked in around the 20th and 21st best safeties in the NFL among league coaches, executives and scouts via ESPN’s @JFowlerESPN . They fell in the “also receiving votes” category, well outside the top 10. pic.twitter.com/BtWqKvcNuw — Zac Stevens (@ZacStevens) July 16, 2026 Player Profile Age: 27 | Experience: Sixth Year | College: USC | Height: 6’0” | Weight: 200 pounds 2025 Statistics : 17 games played with 17 starts. 106 tackles, 6 tackles for loss, 2 sacks, 1 forced fumble, 11 pass deflections. Talanoa Hufanga’s 2026 outlook with the Broncos Hufanga is slated to be the starter opposite of Brandon Jones at safety once again for the Broncos. While most pundits and analysts rank Denver’s backend duo outside of the top ten, I believe they are one of the more diverse and consistent pairings in the NFL. In coverage in ’25, Hufanga allowed just 60-percent of passes his direction to be completed—the second-best mark of his career. I thought he was fundamentally sound in that regard and only allowed three touchdowns through the air. Additionally, his 106 tackles were the most of his career. That ranked second on the Broncos defense last season behind only linebacker Alex Singleton. From Day 1, Hufanga’s versatility and fiery on the field demeanor were a huge asset for the Broncos’ defense. His on the field temperament is palpable. The aggression and penchant for tone-setting hits were an important addition to Vance Joseph’s defense last season. That will continue for the upcoming season. One area of improvement would be generating more turnovers. While Hufanga had a career high 11 pass deflections, he didn’t register any interceptions last season and dropped nearly a half a dozen. If he can create more takeaways, it wouldn’t be a surprise for him to once again earn Pro-Bowl or All-Pro accolades. Final Thoughts Hufanga was a key addition for the Broncos’ defense last year. He is a well-rounded player that performs strongly in coverage and has a nose for the football in run support. I strongly believe he is poised to have a better season in ‘26 with the Broncos than he did last year.

It’s going to be real fun for sure.” That is a big deal to be honest. A team can only go as far as the players in that building and if they are driven by an intense desire for greatness combined with superior talent, then the sky is truly the limit for these guys. I can’t wait for this season to begin. How about you? Horse Tracks

title: Lions S Kerby Joseph offers some reassurance on his health
summary: Detroit Lions rookies report to training camp on Saturday, and veterans will follow on Monday. One of the first steps for players upon their return to the Meijer Performance Center is to get a physical prior to taking the field. That means those who aren’t ready will be placed on the Physically Unable to Perform […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) practices during OTAs at Detroit Lions headquarters and practice facility in Allen Park on Tuesday, June 11, 2024. Detroit Lions rookies report to training camp on Saturday, and veterans will follow on Monday. One of the first steps for players upon their return to the Meijer Performance Center is to get a physical prior to taking the field. That means those who aren’t ready will be placed on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) or Non-Football Injury (NFI) list until they are medically cleared. Many eyes will be on whether Lions safety Kerby Joseph will start camp on the PUP list due to the knee injury he’s been dealing with for nearly an entire year. But Joseph offered some vaguely optimistic words about his current health via Twitter on Saturday morning. Responding to a tweet that was wondering whether Joseph would start training camp on the PUP list, Joseph replied, “How much yall wanna bet im not on there” How much yall wanna bet im not on there 👌🤔 https://t.co/vJsHyjvjR8 — ZEANU REAVES🥷🏿 (@ZUPE31) July 25, 2026 Joseph missed the last 11 games of last season with this knee injury, and the prognosis for his condition has always been murky at best. Surgery apparently has not been an option for his knee, and last season both Joseph and Lions coach Dan Campbell suggested this was something he is always going to have to manage . Even if Joseph avoids the PUP list, it’s hard to know how Detroit will manage his injury in training camp and the preseason. In the spring, Campbell said they didn’t really know what to expect from Joseph’s knee and they’ll really only know for sure once he’s out there on the field testing it. “We’re just slowly building, continuing to strengthen there. He’s getting treatment; he’s done some of these different things in different places to try and help,” Campbell said in June. “So I feel good about that. I feel good about that we’ve done everything we can and so has he. So we won’t know. Honestly, we probably won’t know until we get into the thick of training camp.” The Lions’ first training camp practice is currently scheduled for Wednesday.

title: Do the Lions have the best top-end talent in the NFL?
summary: To reach the ultimate goal in the NFL of winning a Super Bowl, it takes everything in the organization as a whole clicking at the right time. From the top-end talent, all the way down to the members of the practice squad—everyone needs to pull their weight and row in the right direction in order […]
full_text: To reach the ultimate goal in the NFL of winning a Super Bowl, it takes everything in the organization as a whole clicking at the right time. From the top-end talent, all the way down to the members of the practice squad—everyone needs to pull their weight and row in the right direction in order to get where you want to go. For the Detroit Lions, 2026 is certainly shaping up to be a pivotal season, while also being a bit of a transitional year, too. With key veterans such as linebacker Alex Anzalone and left tackle Taylor Decker moving on, the Lions will be leaning on young players to step up and fill those voids. With that said, there is no arguing one aspect of the Lions’ roster, and that is how stacked they are at the top. If you don’t believe me, check out ESPN’s recent series where they polled executives, coaches, and scouts from around the league in order to determine who are the top-10 players at the various positions. And in no real surprise, the Lions came in first, with nine players ranked inside of the top-10 of their respective positions. From the top-ranked tackle in Penei Sewell to the second-ranked running back in Jahmyr Gibbs—the Lions seemingly have an All-Pro-caliber player at nearly every position on the field. That brings us to today’s question of the day: Do the Lions have the best top-end talent in the NFL? My answer: Absolutely. Even if you unfortunately live in Illinois, Wisconsin, or Minnesota, you know the Lions’ top-tier talent is the best in the NFL. You could argue a few other rosters in the league, such as the Philadelphia Eagles or the Kansas City Chiefs, but even then—the Lions’ stars are still very young, with many of them being 25 years old and under. What about you? Where do you think the top-end of the Lions’ roster stands when comparing it to others around the league? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview: Nickel sets mean more opportunities for CBs
summary: In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we shift back to the defensive secondary by examining the Lions’ cornerbacks, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Roger McCreary (21) talks to defensive quality control Dre Thompson during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Friday, May 29, 2026. | Junfu Han / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images In this installment of our Detroit Lions 2026 training camp preview series, we shift back to the defensive secondary by examining the Lions’ cornerbacks, speculating on current and future roles, and discussing how many players from this group could make the 53-man roster. Previous training camp previews: Quarterback: Can Luke Altmyer force a QB3 role? Running back: How RB roles could shift in 2026 Wide receiver: WR depth roles up for grabs Tight end: How many TEs will make the roster? Offensive tackle: Can Blake Miller win the starting RT job? Interior OL: How quickly will Cade Mays adapt to scheme? Defensive tackles: DT has upgraded starters, questionable depth Edge rushers: 4 big questions at the EDGE Linebackers: Adapting the LB room Roster construction Under the Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell regime, the Lions have fluctuated in the number of cornerbacks on the active roster, typically keeping five or six corners active, but have adjusted the room as injuries piled up. Let’s take a look at what they’ve done at corner in the previous five seasons: 2021 : Started the season with six, but ended with just five. 2022 : Repeated the previous season by starting with six and ending with five. 2023 : The Lions opened and ended with seven, but only kept six active on game days. 2024 : They started with six and ended with just four, though three contributors finished the season on injured reserve. 2025 : Opened the season with five corners, but after only a month, injuries mounted, and the room fluctuated between five and seven corners throughout the season, ending with six corners Starter turnover and Nickel defense The Lions’ secondary was forced to undergo a series of changes this offseason; some decisions were purposeful, while others were forced upon them. At outside cornerback, D.J. Reed (10 starts in 2025) returns for 2026, and while he is coming off an injury that cost him nearly two months of the regular season, expectations are that he will enter training camp healthy. Rock Ya-Sin (six starts) re-signed and is expected to open training camp in the starting lineup, as previous starters Terrion Arnold (seven starts) was released following his arrest and Amik Robertson (10 starts) departed in free agency . Ennis Rakestraw returns for his third season in Detroit, but he is coming off an injury that cost him the entire 2025 season. While he has previously challenged for inside and outside roles, newly acquired Roger McCreary started in the slot during spring practices and is expected to stay in that role entering training camp. To round out the room, the Lions re-signed special teams ace Khalil Dorsey and Legion-of-whom hero Nick Whiteside, drafted Keith Abney in the fifth round, and signed UDFA De’Shawn Rucker following the conclusion of the draft. The battleground Will Rock Ya-Sin hold off challengers? Following Arnold’s release, the presumption is that Ya-Sin will open training camp as the starter opposite Reed. He was the preferred choice last season, and stylistically, he is a terrific fit for the Lions’ man-heavy scheme. While he was likely initially signed to fill out the Lions’ outside CB3 role, the drop-off from Arnold (who was full of potential but lacked on-field production) to Ya-Sin isn’t as dramatic as it looks on paper. That being said, Ya-Sin won’t simply be gifted a starting role, and he will face some competition in camp, most notably from former second-round pick Ennis Rakestraw. Injuries have plagued the young corner in his first two seasons in the NFL, but Rakestraw’s spent the last year adding “a bit of bulk” via the Lions’ strength and conditioning staff , and enters camp with a more “dense” frame in order to help his body get prepared for this season. With Rakestraw missing all of last season, it’s easy to forget the toughness, aggression, and energy he plays with. He’s stylistically a very good fit for the Lions’ coverage scheme, and he’s an above-average run defender. His lack of playing time in the NFL will be an obstacle for him to overcome, and likely why Ya-Sin will get the nod over him at the beginning of camp. Ya-Sin could also face competition from Roger McCreary, however… Will an increase in Nickel packages keep McCreary in the slot? The Lions used more base formations (three linebackers) than any team in the NFL last season, and as a result, only deployed a nickel corner on about half their defensive snaps. With a significant shift in the linebacker room, defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard acknowledged that the team plans on leaning on more nickel packages in 2026, which increases the value and opportunities for their cornerbacks this season. McCreary spent spring practices (OTAs and minicamp) working in the slot, but Arnold’s release over the summer has the potential to shake things up. McCreary has the range and experience to challenge Ya-Sin and Rakestraw for a starting role on the outside, but the anticipated increase in nickel subpackages could mean that he may be more valuable sticking inside. We should find out very quickly what the Lions’ plans are for McCreary, once camp practices begin. Any sleeper challengers? Of the remaining cornerbacks on the roster, the biggest wild card is rookie Keith Abney. Widely viewed as a Top 100 player in this draft class, Abney slid to Day 3, and the Lions seized the opportunity to select him. Abney started in the slot for two seasons in college before shifting outside for his final year, giving him valuable experience to compete at multiple spots in the secondary. He’s gritty ( top 30 on the Grit Index with a 9.07 score ), competitive, physical, and productive around the ball due to his elite read-and-react explosion. While his frame (5-foot-10, 187 pounds) and skill set point to him having the potential to challenge for a starting slot role, Abney also possesses traits that will mirror D.J. Reed, suggesting he should also be given an opportunity on the outside. Abney is another player who will see more opportunities with the Lions increasing their use of subpackages. As a rookie, he will have a lot of work to do in order to prove he can be trusted on the field, but his competitiveness, confidence, and developmental upside are too promising to rule out. Do the Lions HAVE to sign a veteran corner? Following Arnold’s release, initial reactions expected the Lions to try to secure a veteran corner for the room. While that is certainly still a possibility, it’s also important to recognize that roster spots could be difficult to find. Reed, Ya-Sin, McCreary, Rakestraw, and Abney should all be heavy favorites to earn a spot on the roster, leaving one or two spots potentially available. Special teams ace Khalil Dorsey should have a strong case to justify one of the remaining spots, but is there another available? If there is room to keep a seventh corner, a veteran could make a lot of sense for depth. Outside corners Marshon Lattimore, Tre’Davious White, and Trevon Diggs remain available free agents who fit the scheme, but have struggled in recent seasons, while Kenny Moore could be an option in the slot if McCreary is shifted into the outside corner competition. So do the Lions HAVE to sign a veteran corner? No. But it’s worth considering, if only for training camp.

title: Packers 2025 Callsheet: Low Red Zone
summary: If you’re new to this series, we’re reviewing how the Green Bay Packers offense performed in 2025 by situation. We’re doing that by building out a call sheet, which I ran down in my initial post. This is the 10th article in the series, where we’re looking at the Low Red Zone. Generally I look at […]
full_text: If you’re new to this series, we’re reviewing how the Green Bay Packers offense performed in 2025 by situation. We’re doing that by building out a call sheet, which I ran down in my initial post . This is the 10th article in the series, where we’re looking at the Low Red Zone. Generally I look at the Low Red Zone as plays between the opponent’s 1-10 yard line, but I wanted to break it down 1 step further this year and bring in a goal line section. Based on some research, I’ve decided that the goal line package should start at the 3 yard line. So, today, we’re looking at Low Red Zone Non-Goal Line (4-10 yard line). In our next post, we’ll look at the goal line. The Packers averaged 2.4 plays per game in this area of the field in 2025, tied for 13th in the league. While their goal line offense comes out looking pretty good, this area of the field was a struggle. Their Success Rate of 46.8% was 16th (right in the middle of the pack), but their TD Rate of 12.8% was 28th in the league. TD Rate in this area isn’t necessarily an indicator of good offenses (the Raiders led the league in TD Rate with 38.2%), you’d like to see more production. If we’re just talking volume stats, the Packers scored 6 TDs in this area of the field in 2025, tied for 28th in the league. The top team was the Jaguars, who scored 19 TDs in this area. That’s 13 more TDs! If you want to be a good red zone scoring team, you need 1 of these 3 things: 1. A freak at WR who you can just throw up some 50/50 balls to, 2. A good running game, or 3. A QB who is a running threat There are, of course, other factors, but the best Red Zone scoring teams in the league generally have at least 1 of those things. That’s especially true outside the goal line. Watson fits the bill of point #1, but he missed half the season. The run game wasn’t great this year, and Love – while a solid scrambler – isn’t the quick-twitch type of runner who can thrive in this area. Provided everyone stays healthy, I think they’ll be a much better team in this area of the field in 2026, but 2025 didn’t see the Packers at their best. We’re looking at 3 plays this week. In this area of the field last year, the Packers had a pass rate of 48.9%, 26th in the league. While normally that’s something I’d frown at, there’s a good reason for that. They had a 32% success rate while passing and a 66.7% success rate while running. However, they had a 20% TD rate while passing and an 8.3% TD rate while running. So I opted to split the difference. We’ve got 1 pass, 1 run and 1 RPO. Pass TE Pop (8.0 YPA, 100% Success) I love this play because it has the presentation of a run in terms of formation. They’re in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) in a YY Wing formation (both TEs tight to the line on the same side of the formation). I don’t have the numbers on what the Packers did out of this specific formation in 2025, but it’s something that worked well for them. In these formations, you’d see Tucker Kraft as the inside man. On run plays, that puts the strongest blocking TE closer to the formation, but it makes him more difficult to cover on pass plays. On the play above, you can see the Commanders leaning heavily on the strong side of the formation. Kraft engages briefly on a block, then disengages and releases into open space. In this area of the field, all you need is one little misstep in the defense to take advantage of. This plays so well off the power run game. Run Inside Zone (4.4 YPA, 80% Success) The fastest path to your destination is a straight line, etc. RPO Inside Zone / Bubble (4.0 YPA, 100% Success) While the Packers RPO game hasn’t been nearly as effective as it used to be, it can still be a weapon in this area of the field. Again, all you need is a slight misstep. The issue with this kind of RPO in the open field is that teams can bait you into throwing the Bubble by showing one defender over the stack, with an overhang defender on that side (aligned between the tackle and the closest receiver). It can look like there’s only one defender, but that overhang is looking to just shoot the gap. That’s tougher in this area of the field – especially against this YY Wing look – as you leave yourself vulnerable to the run. Still, this gives you the option to throw the ball to the bubble if the defense gives you a favorable pre-snap look. The entire idea is to make the defense wrong no matter how they play it, and that can work well down here. title: Colts are taking major gambles heading into the season (part 1)
summary: There is no perfect team in the NFL. No matter how good a team is, it will always have holes. Fielding a 53-man roster that is competent across the board is tough, and that’s assuming everyone stays healthy. The Indianapolis Colts have holes and are leaving themselves open to some major issues as they choose […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward Sr. (7) reacts to a penalty Sunday, Nov. 30, 2025, during a game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. | Christine Tannous/IndyStar / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images There is no perfect team in the NFL. No matter how good a team is, it will always have holes. Fielding a 53-man roster that is competent across the board is tough, and that’s assuming everyone stays healthy. The Indianapolis Colts have holes and are leaving themselves open to some major issues as they choose to cross their fingers and hope everything works out. Let’s start with Daniel Jones. He isn’t healthy, might miss the start of the season, and even when he is at his best, is he good enough? The Colts are expecting him to play like he did to start last year, but that is a major roll of the dice. He isn’t the only player coming back from injury. DeForest Buckner missed time and isn’t getting any younger. At cornerback, the Colts are banking on Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward. After what we saw last year, the over/under on them appearing in games together might be eight if we’re lucky. Oh, and how about Alec Pierce? What is his ankle looking like? Those are some premier players at premier positions. What is the depth behind them? Just the thought probably makes you shiver. The roster has depth, but not at every position. If Jones doesn’t perform or Pierce misses time, the drop-off is severe. This isn’t to say other teams survive losing their best players, but some, like Jones, are overly susceptible to missing time. Ward is one concussion away from calling it quits, and Buckner sounds like he is year-to-year anyway. Another season of injuries could be enough to push him into retirement. The Colts are banking a lot of their hopes on players who either missed extensive time during the season and/or will miss parts of the offseason. That is playing with fire. While the core group of players is essential to all teams, walking into the season with your core on crutches or recovering from so much missed time makes for an uncomfortable gamble.

On transition from College to Pro .. says he feels like a "kid in a candy store" being here with the #Chiefs pic.twitter.com/SSJdU9mSRN — Harold R. title: Andy Reid pleased with having rookie portion of Chiefs camp again
summary: Rookies and quarterbacks for the Kansas City Chiefs reported to Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph on Friday for the initial part of the team’s training camp this season. The rookie camp portion had been a staple of head coach Andy Reid’s program for over a decade with the Chiefs. Last season, however, Reid […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - JANUARY 04: Head coach Andy Reid of the Kansas City Chiefs speaks to the media after the game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images Rookies and quarterbacks for the Kansas City Chiefs reported to Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph on Friday for the initial part of the team’s training camp this season. The rookie camp portion had been a staple of head coach Andy Reid’s program for over a decade with the Chiefs. Last season, however, Reid bypassed the first stage and had rookies and veterans report together. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Reid left no doubt that he much prefers the phase-in. He also confirmed that the state of the roster demanded a return of an early report date. Almost a third of Kansas City’s current 90-man roster is comprised of rookies. The youth of the roster should allow for plenty of work to go around over the next two days. “That’s the primary thing, the rookies,” said Reid. “I just thought it was necessary. I didn’t like not doing it last year after I got done with it. It’s a good thing for the quarterbacks. It’s a good thing for the rookies coming in. We do have more numbers this year, so it allows us to get more reps that I think will benefit us.” By having the short time for coaches to work specifically with rookies, Reid believes that the players can get an extra refresher on what was learned in the offseason before the full squad is in meeting rooms later in the week. The coach sees the college atmosphere — with the infamous dorm accommodations — as conducive to learning. “It’s a little different,” Reid explained. “It’s great to be back with the cinderblocks surrounding you. It puts them right back as freshmen in college. I don’t think they’ll be too shocked by that part. The workload is going to be tough, obviously. They’ll push through it. “These three days are great for rookies to give them an instruction to offense again , the defense again [and] special teams again where you can slow it down a little bit. You don’t have a ton of numbers, but you have enough where they can get reps. But you’ve got to slow it down because of numbers and the heat and all that to get work done there. It gives them a nice little ramp up. Then, they get another review once the veterans get in of basically the same plays for those first couple of days. “It can be beneficial as long — as you are focused in on it.” With quarterbacks also reporting early, the Chiefs have another beneficial ramp-up period. The early story of the NFL this season will be the health of star quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who suffered multiple torn knee ligaments in December. Reid revealed in his opening comments Friday that Mahomes has been cleared to practice. Still, the extra time the quarterback can get on the field is a bonus. “The nice thing about having this rookie camp is you can kind of gradually build it up,” Reid acknowledged. “Then, he gets a day off normally that third day anyway. We’ll get an idea where he’s at there.”

title: 51 Days until Chiefs football, we are ‘R Mason Thomas’ days away
summary: We are 51 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 51 jersey will be worn by rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas, who could have a key role in upgrading the pass rush in 2026. He is taking the jersey […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: R Mason Thomas #51 of the Kansas City Chiefs on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images We are 51 days away from the Kansas City Chiefs ‘ season-opening game against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football” in Week 1. The No. 51 jersey will be worn by rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas, who could have a key role in upgrading the pass rush in 2026. He is taking the jersey over from Mike Danna, who is now with the Buffalo Bills . Here are some all-time Chiefs who came to mind when thinking of players who have worn No. 51: The memorable No. 51s in franchise history Jim Lynch (1967 – 1977) Mike Danna (2020 – 2025) Frank Zombo (2013 – 2018) Charles Jackson (1978 – 1984) Scott Fujita (2002 – 2004) Lynch was drafted by the Chiefs in the second round of the 1967 draft as a middle linebacker out of Notre Dame. He famously competed with legendary Chiefs linebacker Willie Lanier for the middle linebacker spot on the team; head coach Hank Stram paired the two together as roommates for training camp and road trips. Lanier would win the job, becoming the first black middle linebacker in professional football history, and Lynch would become a Pro Bowl outside linebacker, staying roommates with Lanier for the next eight seasons. The two were key factors in winning Super Bowl IV. 51: The number of team rushing yards against the Titans in Week 16 last season In the first game without starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes last season, the offense laid as big of an egg as it had all season, especially in the run game. 51 rushing yards as a team were the second-lowest total of the season, a putrid effort considering the interior three of the starting offensive line was still intact. It’s a reminder that the flaws on the offense were deeply rooted last season, and the dramatic changes to personnel and the coaching staff reflect that. The offense shouldn’t look as inept as it did in the absence of Mahomes. There needs to be a stronger foundation in the scheme and the ability to run the ball if Mahomes were to miss time this year.

title: What’s the ceiling on the Rams edge unit?
summary: Blockbuster trades have punctuated the news about the Los Angeles Rams defense in 2026. The edge unit, already a team strength, took another step forward with the addition of six-time All-Pro Myles Garrett. For the soon-approaching season, he be complimented by a deep bench. The edge position has evolved from defensive ends of the past, […]
full_text: Myles Garrett (95) at Rams practice (Photo by David Crane/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Blockbuster trades have punctuated the news about the Los Angeles Rams defense in 2026. The edge unit, already a team strength, took another step forward with the addition of six-time All-Pro Myles Garrett. For the soon-approaching season, he be complimented by a deep bench. The edge position has evolved from defensive ends of the past, they were always the most athletic of the big guys in front, but now are certified playmakers that can change the flow and even its outcome of game with a single play. With explosive plays and forcing turnovers being such harbinger of victory, it’s almost a necessity that every successful team boasts game breaker off the edge. The 2026 Rams are blessed with a deep edge room featuring two potential All-Pro’s, complimented by a pair of backups that are short on experience, but long on effort/potential and primed for rotational success. Behind those Top 4, there’s a handful of players pushing for their slice of the pie. Let’s meet them. The new guy Myles Garrett 6’4” 272 lb. A lot has been expected of Garrett. He was a Top 5 high school recruit, garnered All-American accolades in all three college seasons, and was the Number 1 overall pick in the 2017 NFL Draft. Although a late training camp injury kept him from being a Day 1 starter and shelved him for five games, he’s produced at a Hall of Fame level since. He’s booked double-digit sacks in eight straight seasons. He’s already 20th all-time in sacks and 12th all-time in tackles for loss. Clearly a generational talent, now it’s Rams fans turn for high expectations. Garrett is in his prime and will have a superior cast of supporting characters. Fans may see more four-down fronts from the L.A. defense, because Garrett has played predominantly with a hand in the dirt and outside the the shoulders of opposing offensive tackles. Returnees Byron Young 6’2” 250 lb. In the final year of his rookie contract, Young has proven to be a durable, steady edge providing a solid return on his mid-Round 3 draft stake. In 2025, according to Next Gen Stats , he led the defensive front starters in tackles for loss (12), hustle stops (12), sacks (12), QB hits (29), and pass rush pressure percentage (14.1). He was 2nd in total pressures (54) and stops (62). He also dropped into coverage on 121 of his 813 snaps (15%). A stellar blend of speed and power, Young was a raw prospect coming out of college and has consistently worked to upgrade his game.That improvement shows in his year-to-year on-field production. At his best, he is explosive off the snap and uses good pad level to put blockers on their heels.You can see on his 2025 film that he has improved his hand strikes/swipes and now uses/stacks more moves. Enough speed and dip to get around the corner. Not just a pass rusher, Young has become a stout against the run and his burst in pursuit leads to many hustle tackles. Decent in pass coverage, I’ve never liked the Rams dropping their edges into coverage so often, but he’s got the agility and change of direction. Byron Young has been the most dangerous member of a DEEP Rams edge rushing rotation so far this season. His 43.5% pass rush win rate is 2nd in the NFL, behind only Myles Garrett 🤯 pic.twitter.com/55keTnH8xw — NFL Draft Files (@NFL_DF) September 16, 2025 Josiah Stewart – 6’1” 249 lbs The narrative on Stewart coming out of college was that he was a Top 50 prospect, but for whatever reason, chose not to test at the NFL Combine or Michigan Pro Day. In a private, individual testing/workout, he performed poorly. He fell into the Rams lap at #90. He’s a bit under-sized, but plays much bigger and fits the Rams inclination for players that have success at smaller schools and the continue that production at a higher level of competition. The Rams got Stewart’s feet wet early, he played in all 20 games as a rookie, 374 snaps on defense and another 121 on special teams. His game film doesn’t show a lack of athleticism, he looks to have good get-off and enough speed to get around tackles outside. His pursuit speed looks to be above-average and bolstered by good angles and 100 percent effort. Out in space and into coverage, he appears to be agile and loose-limbed. While he still needs some strength work to stack and shed bigger pro’s, Stewart is cognizant of where the ball is/going and flows to it naturally. Desjuan Johnson – 6’2” 285 lb. Johnson was drafted out of Toledo in Round 7 of 2022 as an interior player, he lined up primarily between the tackles in college. He made the Rams opening roster in his first two seasons and was employed inside. In mostly mop-up work, he saw action in 21 games and logged 207 defensive reps. For 2025, Johnson was moved outside to edge. The Rams previously had some success transitioning another athletic defensive lineman, Michael Hoecht, to the perimeter. It took over half the season, but when Johnson became comfortable with the switch, from Week 14 through the playoffs he was part of the edge rotation. While not a gifted athlete, Johnson does show good get-off, violent hands, and good contact balance. His mass was below par when playing inside and he could be moved, now standing up on the outside, he sets a strong edge and has the strength and hand technique too fight off blockers. Uses his basic inside pass rush move, bullrush, swim, chop and has nice head/shoulder jab feint. Not a bendy player that going use speed to get the corner and flatten out. how to bull rush AND keep contain … keep head up, don't get sucked inside well done by Desjuan Johnson–gets a QB knockdown pic.twitter.com/eAyYEjQWoD — Jim Youngblood 53 (@53_jim70721) January 5, 2026 Keir Thomas – 6’2” 272 lb. Somewhat similar to Johnson, Thomas was a hand in the dirt lineman in college. Signed as an undrafted free agent in 2022, he made the opening roster, but has bounced back and forth from the practice squad. He spent all of 2025 on the Injured Reserve List. In three partial seasons, he’s played in 17 games with one start and charted 204 defensive snaps and 147 more on special teams. Steady well-rounded game and plays with full effort. The problem is that he doesn’t have the mass to play inside in the NFL and lacks the athleticism to be valuable stand-up edge. Good handwork, plays with leverage, and naturally flows towards the ball, staying engaged lets him make back door tackles.. Good linear speed and burst to shoot gaps.Solid tackler, but lumbers a bit when navigating space in coverage. Undrafted practice squad battle Tomon Fox – 6’2” 253 lb. Signed as a free agent on June 2 when the Rams placed 2026 undrafted edge Eddie Walls on the Injured Reserve List. Fox treks west after four seasons with the New York Giants. Signed as a UDFA in 2022, he bounced between their active roster and practice squad, playing in 37 games with two starts and logging 621 defensive snaps along with another 564 on special teams. Fox plays an effort-based game and while his skills are enough to compete for a roster spot, they are not enough to make an real impact. Not a bad player to have at the bottom of the roster. He offers a veteran’s approach, can spell staters off the edge, and play some special teams. He’s also familiar with moving up and down from the roster to practice squad. Darryl Peterson – 6’1” 248 lb. Compact build although a bit short. Peterson meets the NFL size/athleticism standards in arm length, speed/burst, agility/change of direction, flexibility/balance, and upper/lower body explosion. Although he played standing up early in his career, Wisconsin miscast him as an interior player with a hand in the dirt. Reportedly bulked up to play inside last season, often lining up as a 3tech, shading between the guard and tackle. On film, the violence in his hands stands out, he chops and swipes blockers attempts to strike or latch on. When lineman can get…

title: Rams’ defensive backs coach has some interesting history
summary: Jimmy Lake, the LA Rams’ newly appointed defensive backs coordinator who also serves as the pass game coordinator, has a history with the Rams’ newly acquired cornerback, Trent McDuffie. Jimmy Lake was Trent McDuffie’s coach during his three-year stay at the University of Washington, first as the Huskies’ defensive coordinator in 2019, then as the […]
full_text: Sep 18, 2021; Seattle, Washington, USA; Washington Huskies head coach Jimmy Lake reacts following a play against the Arkansas State Red Wolves during the third quarter at Alaska Airlines Field at Husky Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images Jimmy Lake, the LA Rams’ newly appointed defensive backs coordinator who also serves as the pass game coordinator, has a history with the Rams’ newly acquired cornerback, Trent McDuffie. Jimmy Lake was Trent McDuffie’s coach during his three-year stay at the University of Washington, first as the Huskies’ defensive coordinator in 2019, then as the head coach in 2020 and ’21. In 2019, McDuffie’s first with Washington, Lake’s defense limited opposing offenses to 19.4 points per game despite losing nine defensive starters from the previous year. In 2021, McDuffie earned All-Pac-12 First Team honors. McDuffie knows the work it’s going to take to play in Jimmy’s system ; “(He’s going to) truly pour into this DB room, which I love,” McDuffie said about Jimmy on June 8. “Coming from college, Coach Lake was someone that taught me how to play corner, taught me how to see the football field from a coach’s perspective. He’s going to add a lot of great things to this DB room that is young, that is hungry, that wants to get better. He’s a perfectionist, and I think we need to have a coach that’s a perfectionist and that’s going to work on the details day in and day out.” An interesting side note in Trent McDuffie’s full-circle acquisition by the Rams: he and Quentin Lake (no relation to Jimmy) played together on the same high school team, Mater Dei, in Santa Ana for one season. View this post on Instagram I’m thinking they got a deal on those helmets. Jimmy Lake (cue music) This list, compiled by Pro Football Reference, perfectly illustrates the arduous journey coaches can take to reach the NFL. As I’m researching his journey, there’s a Beatles tune playing in my head. Kudos to anyone who guesses the tune and posts in the comments! At Eastern Washington, his alma mater, Lake was a defensive backs coach from 2000-2003, after which he moved up to the Washington Huskies for one year, still with defensive backs, and then to Montana State. At Montana, Lake’s defense led the Big Sky conference, allowing just 165.6 passing yards per game . The NFL was watching, and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers signed him as their assistant DB coach, where he stayed for two years working under Monte Kiffin. Onward and upward to the Detroit Lions as their DB coach. Those are the infamous 0-16 Lions. Joe Barry, the Lions’ defensive coordinator at the time, also got his feet wet under the legendary Kiffin. Back to Tampa working with Raheem Morris in Morris’ first head coaching position for two years. Yet another good defensive brain to learn from. From Tampa he returned to college ball for ten years. Two years at Boise St. and back once again to Washington. Lake rose up through the ranks, finally becoming the head coach following the unexpected resignation of Chris Petersen. In his first year as a head coach, in the covid shortened four game season, the Huskies went 3-1 and won the Pac-12 North Division title. In his six prior seasons at Washington – two as defensive backs coach, two as co-defensive coordinator and the last two as defensive coordinator – Lake has earned a reputation as a teacher, recruiter and tactician, helping the UW become one of the strongest and most consistent defensive teams – and specifically one of the top secondaries – in the nation. The team’s performance and a sideline scuffle led to Lake’s firing at the end of the following season. Back to the NFL 2023, Lake returns to the NFL with the Rams as Assistant Head Coach, perhaps at the suggestion of Raheem Morris. At the end of the year, he follows Morris to Atlanta as the Defensive Coordinator, where Morris has been named head coach. The year did not go well; Morris was fired, and Lake returned to the Rams in 2025 as Sr. Defensive Assistant. The 2025 Rams defense was ‘almost good enough’. The defensive backs, in particular, have taken the brunt of the blame for the team’s inability to hold late leads. The head office did some ‘self-scouting’ in the post-season and rectified the DB situation by acquiring 3 time Pro Bowler Trent McDuffie and his partner in the backfield from Kansas City, Jaylen Watson. Jimmy Lake was elevated to defensive backs coordinator this year, in addition to his role as pass game coordinator. The front office has given him and Chris Shula all of the missing pieces to make this defense one of the best in the league. Nothing short of a Super Bowl can be called a success this year, for the Rams, and the defense will play a major role in achieving that goal. Jimmy Lake has a glorious opportunity to finally achieve a lifelong goal.

title: How Rams will change training camp to aid Ty Simpson’s development
summary: First-round draft pick Ty Simpson inked his rookie contract with the Los Angeles Rams. He’ll battle with Stetson Bennett to earn the rights to backup Matthew Stafford. As players report to training camp, it seems the Rams have a plan to both manage Stafford’s workload and provide additional opportunities to Simpson in order to aid […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: Ty Simpson #15 of the Los Angeles Rams sets up to pass during organized team activities workout at Rams Village at the Warner Center on May 28, 2026 in Woodland Hills, California. (Photo by Kevin Terrell/Getty Images) | Getty Images First-round draft pick Ty Simpson inked his rookie contract with the Los Angeles Rams. He’ll battle with Stetson Bennett to earn the rights to backup Matthew Stafford. As players report to training camp, it seems the Rams have a plan to both manage Stafford’s workload and provide additional opportunities to Simpson in order to aid in his development. Nate Atkins from The Athletic touched on this Saturday : The plan for Simpson is to sit and learn behind Stafford for as long as the reigning MVP continues to play. The Rams feel as if he could use that learning after starting just one season at Alabama, when he led the Crimson Tide to the second round of the College Football Playoff and finished with 28 touchdown passes and five interceptions… Simpson will see some reps this summer as Stafford manages a degenerative back issue. The Rams have broken training camp into four-day blocks where Stafford will practice on the second and third days while resting on the first and fourth days. Stafford will not participate in the team’s first practice on Sunday. Simpson will use this training camp, as well as three preseason games, to try to beat out Stetson Bennett for the No. 2 quarterback role. Jimmy Garoppolo had held that spot for the past two seasons but is a free agent considering retirement. The Rams have seemingly drawn the conclusion after watching Stafford miss the entirety of last year’s camp and then going on to win the NFL’s MVP award that the veteran probably doesn’t need much practice. You can’t argue with the results. Similar to how Jimmy Garoppolo kept the train on tracks in 2025, this approach now creates opportunities that otherwise wouldn’t be there for Bennett and Simpson to train with the starters. It’s also more straightforward to evaluate quarterback play when they are operating with a strong supporting cast. Stafford could sit out half of Rams practices— or at least that is the plan for the first week of training camp . That means plenty of time in the spotlight for Simpson. It’s time for the rookie to put on a show .

title: Re-examining the Rams’ need, or lack thereof, for another receiver
summary: If you subscribe to The Athletic and were shocked at what you read this morning in Daniel Popper’s “Best Fits” column about free agent wide receivers, you weren’t alone. As TST’s Danny Stone pointed out in this morning’s Random Ramsdom, Popper wrote that the Rams are the best fit for former San Francisco 49er and, […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 2: Jordan Whittington #88 of the Los Angeles Rams and Davante Adams #17 get set during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at SoFi Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images If you subscribe to The Athletic and were shocked at what you read this morning in Daniel Popper’s “Best Fits” column about free agent wide receivers, you weren’t alone. As TST’s Danny Stone pointed out in this morning’s Random Ramsdom , Popper wrote that the Rams are the best fit for former San Francisco 49er and, most recently, Washington Commander Deebo Samuel. Not only was that a surprising match, but it doesn’t jive with what the Rams are apparently planning for at wide receiver this season. Samuel has been a productive player in the past, of course, even earing a first-team All-Pro nod in 2021. But that was five years ago now, and the reputation that precedes Samuel is far greater than his actual impact on the field now. He wasn’t terrible for Washington last season, posting 72 receptions for 727 yards and five touchdowns, but he’s now another year older and still has the same issues he’s always had, just with further diminished speed and athleticism. This is a player that has never been a strong man-coverage beater and thus has always needed his play callers to manufacture touches for him. ESPN’s Receiver Score metrics aren’t foolproof by any means and the stats do include some noise, but their 2025 grading does paint at least a broad picture of who Samuel is right now. Who is that? It’s a player who tied for 97th out of 110 graded wide receivers in “open” score, or how often a receiver is in position to make a catch even if they’re not targeted. It doesn’t feel like the juice is worth the squeeze for a Rams team that already has one of the best offenses in the NFL and doesn’t need to add more gimmicks to create explosives, move the ball consistently or score. It would be one thing to take a flier is Los Angeles had a paltry assortment of weapons, but that’s clearly not the case, and it’s not worth developing more hyper-specific touches for what could be the Rams’ sixth option. Peyton Manning was absolutely disgusted about a pass hitting Deebo Samuel in the facemask and turning into an interception. 🏈 🎙️ #NFL #MNF pic.twitter.com/HpvO6qFQp5 — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 28, 2025 Overall, the Rams have made it obvious so far that they’re content with the group they have at wide receiver. Ty Simpson’s finally signed rookie deal eats into some of their available cap space and an Aaron Donaald return would obviously swallow most of what’s left. But there are enough options out there who wouldn’t cost an arm and a leg that if L.A. had wanted to add another receiver at some point this offseason, it could have. This roster has a clear hierarchy both in terms of pass catchers and offensive contributors in general, and it’s hard to see a transformative role opening for anyone that Les Snead could go out and sign today. Puka Nacua is one of the five best receivers in the NFL, and Davante Adams is a potential Hall of Famer who is still easily among the best WR2s in the league. Colby Parkinson is going to be on the field a ton at tight end, and plenty of other players in that position group will get run in heavier personnel packages (such as the recently re-signed Tyler Higbee or second-round pick Max Klare). You know the Rams are going to run the ball and run it effectively. Does a guy like Samuel slot in at the back of that pack and actually get you closer to a championship? Or Stefon Diggs, Keenan Allen, Zay Jones or any other veteran wide receiver still looking for a home, for that matter. Jordan Whittington, meanwhile, is already in place and a perfectly suitable option as the No. 3 wide receiver, given what the Rams need out of that spot. He’s a strong blocker and that’s vital to the success of this offense, and it’s not like he’s an unplayable pass catcher, given his 62% career success rate (according to Pro-Football-Reference’s system) and the 41% of his targets that become first downs or touchdowns (all first downs in his case, to be fair). That’s just shy of Diggs’ career rate and above that of Samuel. He isn’t a superstar and almost certainly won’t be given the guys in front of him, but his tangible and intangible traits make him a natural fit for this position group. Would it be nice to have a third elite receiver that didn’t need to get the ball constantly? Sure, who wouldn’t want that? But while that’s been a need or a personnel target some analysts around the NFL have pushed for the Rams all offseason, it’s simply not an important need, and the guy they’ve already got is more that fit for the role.

I recently spoke to Brent Taylor, an Alabama blogger, about Simpson’s four years with the Crimson Tide . He speaks highly of Simpson’s ability to read a defense and to consume an NFL playbook quickly, the type of skills that should translate well for Sean McVay. title: With size, physicality, Roman Hemby can make run at Raiders’ roster spot
summary: Ashton Jeanty is the unquestioned top tailback on the depth chart as the Las Vegas Raiders enter all-important training camp. But what’s the pecking order behind the Silver & Black’s prized running back? That’s one of the questions slated to be answered when Las Vegas as a whole comes together on July 28 when veteran […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Henderson, NV, USA; Las Vegas Raiders running back Roman Hemby (37) carries the ball during minicamp at Intermountain Health Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | Kirby Lee-Imagn Images Ashton Jeanty is the unquestioned top tailback on the depth chart as the Las Vegas Raiders enter all-important training camp. But what’s the pecking order behind the Silver & Black’s prized running back? That’s one of the questions slated to be answered when Las Vegas as a whole comes together on July 28 when veteran players join the rookies (who reported this past Thursday). From there, the Raiders engage in several practices before a trio of preseason clashes starting on August 13 versus the visiting Arizona Cardinals. Let’s start with the current running backs on the roster then shift to preliminary pecking order, and where the competition lies. Joining Jeanty, the sixth overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft, are: 2026 fourth-rounder Mike Washington Jr. out of Arkansas, 2024 sixth-rounder Dylan Laube, and undrafted free agents Chris Collier (2024) and Roman Hemby (2026). Interestingly enough, the way each tailback name is listed, is the preliminary pecking order. And the competition that looms is for that RB3 role that Laube currently has a grip on. But out of the backend trio of Laube, Collier, and Hemby, it’s the latter that brings intriguing size and physicality that other two don’t. By The Numbers Roman Hemby, Running Back, Indiana 2025: 16 games, 230 carries, 1,120 yards, 7 touchdowns; 17 receptions, 165 yards; 9 kick returns, 203 yards. Career: (2021-25; Maryland and Indiana), 58 games, 711 carries, 3,467 yards, 29 touchdowns; 129 receptions, 1,086 yards, 5 touchdowns; 16 kick returns, 287 yards. #Raiders UDFA RB Roman Hemby has the talent to carve out a change-of-pace role alongside Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr., especially as a receiver. A dynamic playmaker staying tied to Fernando Mendoza 👀 pic.twitter.com/s1TpSY9kLX — Nick Walters (@nickwalt) April 29, 2026 Spending most of his collegiate career at Maryland before a standout 2025 campaign during Indiana’s national championship run, Hemby stands 6-feet and 210 pounds and offers a more natural, physical, between-the-tackles power style than Laube or Collier. Alongside Hoosier backfield mate Kaelon Black (selected by the San Francisco 49ers in the third round of the 2026 draft; 90th overall), Hemby helped power Indiana’s ground game with a team-leading 230 carries for 1,120 yards with seven end zone visits. Black led the Hoosiers with 10 rushing touchdowns (alongside 1,040 yards on 186 carries). Both provided Indiana with grinder-type tailbacks who welcomed contact and typically fell forward for additional yards when eventually brought down. Hemby, in particular, was the more violent of the two Indiana halfbacks and thrives as a decisive runner in both gap and zone schemes. He’s a reliable back to pound the rock inside and brings added value of pass protector and pass catcher out of the backfield. Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak is installing his preferred wide/outside zone scheme in Las Vegas, but he (alongside offensive line coach Rick Dennison and offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko) adapted to incorporate more gap/power elements into the ground game during their respective times with the Seattle Seahawks last season. Which makes a running back with Hemby’s profile and traits an attractive option. Jeanty and Washington bring elements of drive through contact as physical power runners who can thrive between the tackles or one-cut and dash outside for yardage. Unlike Laube and Collier who are more agile ball carriers who don’t have the physical makeup for the collision style the aforementioned tailbacks bring to the table. Laube (5-foot-9 and 204 pounds) is a pass-catching type runner who has the hands and foot quickness, but hasn’t put it together for two previous Raiders coaching staffs to earn any significant offensive snaps (just 29 total and he’s got eight career carries for nine yards and three receptions for 18 yards to show for it). Collier, meanwhile, stands 5-foot-10 and 203 pounds and is of similar ilk physically and trait-wise, and he’s logged 19 career offensive snaps (16 with the Raiders in 2025) and has five carries for 12 yards and one reception for minus-four yards as he heads into Year 3 like Laube. Thus, the opportunity is there for Hemby to showcase the skillsets that made him a dependable running back at Indiana as the Raiders embark on training camp and upcoming preseason tilts. New TDL just dropped with @MHolder95 starting to look at the UDFA class with RB Roman Hemby and Edge rusher Cian Slone. Check it out with the link below! pic.twitter.com/MUfYxdKfY7 — Marcus Johnson (@TheMarcJohnNFL) May 17, 2026 As our Matt Holder penned this past Tuesday, Washington has the clear-cut path towards a roster spot and complementary role to Jeanty as RB2 . And I agree, unless the Arkansas speed/power back face plants as the rest of the offseason proceeds, he’s likeliest to earn the backup role and provide a change-of-pace option behind Jeanty. The rest of the group has plenty to prove, however. Despite heading into Year 3, Laube and Collier remain unproven products at age 26, and of course, as an undrafted free agent, Hemby (23 years old) is even more neophyte coming from Indiana to Las Vegas. There’s one particular area where Laube has an edge over Collier and Hemby, however: Special teams work. With 33 kick returns for 855 yards (long of 38), the New Hampshire product was one of the primary return specialists alongside veteran tailback Raheem Mostert (23 kick returns for 673 yards; long of 54). Laube also notched five special teams tackles and was called out by new special teams coordinator Joe DeCamillis earlier this offseason. “I think he’s done a great job throughout the OTAs,” DeCamillis said of Laube . “He’s another one that’s really, really sharp, gets the game and he knows the way he’s going to make it is by the more he can do, and he’s accentuated that all the way through camp. I really like him so far. … I think he’s going to be a good player for us.” Collier and Hemby are no strangers to special teams work, either. In Hemby’s case, he was a core special teamer at both Maryland and Indiana and returned nine kickoffs for 203 yards. And displaying both prowess in DeCamillis’ and Kubiak’s respective units is Hemby’s best path towards a 53-man roster spot. It’s viable that Laube locks in as a special teams option while Hemby slots in as RB3 behind Jeanty and Washington. It’s also possible that Hemby doesn’t make any traction. This is what makes the training camp progress intriguing.
