title: Las Vegas Raiders Mailbag: Could Jackson Powers-Johnson be surprise roster cut during training camp?
summary: Training camp is finally here as the rookies on the Las Vegas Raiders’ roster reported on Thursday, and the veterans will join them this upcoming Tuesday. The Raiders also had some good news just ahead of camp with Jermod McCoy and Fernando Mendoza signing their contracts, so the entire team should be in attendance to […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - NOVEMBER 02: Jackson Powers-Johnson #58 of the Las Vegas Raiders warms up before a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Allegiant Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Chris Unger/Getty Images) | Getty Images Training camp is finally here as the rookies on the Las Vegas Raiders’ roster reported on Thursday, and the veterans will join them this upcoming Tuesday. The Raiders also had some good news just ahead of camp with Jermod McCoy and Fernando Mendoza signing their contracts, so the entire team should be in attendance to kick off the summer practice sessions, barring any surprises next week. On that note, let’s get to this week’s mailbag! Raiderguy68 Maybe its too broad a question, on the brink of training camp. Who do you forsee as possibly the biggest surprise in regards to not being on the 53-man roster to start the season? That includes trades or practice squad designations. Kinda wondering if JPJ could be a trade candidate if things don’t go well in training camp. A: Jackson Powers-Johnson has been a popular subject when it comes to this topic during the offseason, especially after the Raiders signed a new starting center (Tyler Linderbaum) and used another third-round pick on a guard (Trey Zuhn III). I definitely agree with the thought that Powers-Johnson will be a trade candidate if he doesn’t win one of the two open starting interior offensive line spots during training camp. With Zuhn and Caleb Rogers both having more years left on their rookie contracts than JPJ does, the organization has a pair of young guards to develop outside of the 2024 second-round pick. So if he’s not starting, there’s less reason to keep him on the roster, especially since that likely means Rogers or Zuhn is already ahead of Powers-Johnson on the depth chart. That being said, I think JPJ should win one of the starting jobs because he’s the most talented lineman in the competition. But he has to prove it, and he’s been inconsistent so far. To be clear, I’d imagine he’d get traded rather than being cut outright. The return would probably be pretty minimal, but I’d be willing to bet that some team liked him enough during the draft a couple of years ago to be up for buying low and bet on his potential. As for other potential surprise cuts, I dove into this a little more than a week ago and listed five players (other than JPJ) who could be on the chopping block. Probably the biggest shocker would be Malcolm Koonce! Nunchucks Hey Matt…There’s going to be a position group in need due to injuries or inadequate play in camp…DT, WR, FS and LB depth come to mind…What group do you see as the biggest weakness that the Raiders need to address and who would you like the Raiders to bring in to help out?…Thank You! A: I lean toward the offensive line, and defensive tackle isn’t too far behind. The other three positions you mentioned are certainly up there, too. However, the sticking point for me is that there are a lot of young players who I’d like to see get playing time during the season to help gauge if they can be part of the long-term plan. We already went over the o-line, and the interior d-line is full of young guys outside of Adam Butler and Benito Jones. Wide receiver has Jack Bech, Malik Benson and Dont’e Thornton, while the linebacker depth includes the Bergs, both of whom are still on their rookie contracts. Granted, the options are limited at free safety; more on that later. So, it comes down to this: In a season where we’re expecting the Raiders to be rebuilding (i.e., long shots to be playoff contenders), would you rather see old guys on one-year contracts like Devin White, Jamal Adams and Elandon Roberts, or youngins who are trying to prove themselves and have a future with the organization? I’m going with the latter, which is why I’d rather see the Raiders stay away from adding veterans who are available at the end of July and stick with the roster as is. Raiderjoe English version: I just watched your TDL film analysis of Polamao and Stukes. If we all agree that neither Polamao nor Chinn can play as a deep safety on a full-time basis, does that mean Stukes is our only option? The thing is, no matter how many of his Arizona games I watch, he spends about 95% of his snaps close to the line of scrimmage rather than playing deep. We can’t draft the best slot/apex defender in the class and then move him to deep safety when he has barely played there. I want him around the action, where he can make the biggest impact. And even if they plan to rotate post-snap or move pieces around, what happens if Stukes gets injured? I don’t see that they’ve really thought through an alternative. I still believe their plan was to strengthen the slot/apex position, which is why they brought in both a veteran like Taron Johnson and a rookie like Stukes. But I don’t see anyone on the roster who is a true answer at deep safety. A: This was the reason why Treydan Stukes wasn’t on my radar much heading into the draft; he was a nickelback in college and only took a handful of snaps at free safety. Ironically, after trading for Taron Johnson, I thought the other Arizona safety, Genesis Smith, would be more of a target for John Spytek since Smith was the Wildcats’ deep defender. However, Spytek opted for the better overall player and is taking a flier on Stukes’ versatility. In other words, you’re 100 percent correct that the second-round pick primarily played in the box in college and is a projection at free safety. But if you want him on the field in year one, the clearest path is on the backend of the defense. Jeremy Chinn is the starting strong safety and can play big nickel, while Johnson can fill the slot corner role, and a big question mark exists at free safety. For what it’s worth, I think Stukes has the traits to become a good deep defender in the NFL. He has good instincts, is fast (ran a 4.33 40 at the combine after tearing an ACL in 2024), shows good ball skills (f our interceptions, six PDs last year), and is willing to downhill and mix it up in the running game. On top of that, I think his skill set might actually translate better at free safety than at nickel because I’m not a big fan of his change of direction skills and short-area quickness, both of which are necessary to cover shifty slot receivers in the league. Granted, you could be onto something where maybe the plan is to have Stukes take over at nickel in the future. Chinn’s contract expires at the end of the year, and Johnson’s deal has two more years on it, but 2027 is more like a team option since the Raiders can cut him without taking a dead cap hit, per Over The Cap . But that would just mean free safety is a need again next spring because the cupboard is pretty bare. If Stukes or Isaiah Pola-Mao isn’t lining up at free safety, option C right now is Tristin McCollum, who has been in the league since 2022 and has played less than 500 regular-season snaps in his career. Dalton Johnson has some experience on the backend of the defense, but Johnson profiles more like a strong safety/big nickel to take over for Chinn. So, in my opinion, Stukes is the best option at free safety. If anyone is interested, here’s a link to the Tape Don’t Lie episode referenced in the question. Q: Should we take Klint Kubiak and Kirk Cousins at their word; i.e., the best QB out of camp will be the one to start. Suppose that QB is Aiden O’Connell. How does that change the narrative? A: If O’Connell is the best quarterback in training camp, then that makes him a good trade asset for the Raiders. The organization committed itself to Fernando Mendoza for at least two to three years by taking Mendoza No. 1 overall in the draft, ending any hopes that O’Connell has a future in Las Vegas if he wants to be a starter in the NFL since he’s entering a contract year. I’m sure Spytek is hoping AOC balls out in the preseason because that increases his trade value. But the situation and the narrative doesn’t…

title: Raiders News: Jon Gruden gives Las Vegas harsh reality with AFC West prediction for 2026 season
summary: For better or worse, Jon Gruden will always be connected to the Las Vegas Raiders and will have a strong voice when it comes to the team. He did have two stints as the franchise’s head coach and helped guide four playoff teams in eight seasons with the club, if you give him credit for […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - OCTOBER 10: Head coach John Gruden of the Las Vegas Raiders reacts on the sideline during a game against the Chicago Bears at Allegiant Stadium on October 10, 2021 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images For better or worse, Jon Gruden will always be connected to the Las Vegas Raiders and will have a strong voice when it comes to the team. He did have two stints as the franchise’s head coach and helped guide four playoff teams in eight seasons with the club, if you give him credit for the 2021 season, after all. On Friday, Gruden, who has been working for Barstool Sports since Novemember 2024, recently appeared on FS1’s “Wake Up Barstool” show and gave his prediction for how the AFC West will unfold in the 2026 season, giving the Raiders a harsh reality in the process (h/t Raiders Lead on X ). Former #Raiders HC @BarstoolGruden dropped his AFC West predictions for this season, predicting the #Raiders to finish last in the division 😔 "I think the Raiders are going to improve, but unfortunately for the silver and black this is a very tough division with established… pic.twitter.com/QWWxo8jkV8 — Raiders Lead (@RaidersLead) July 24, 2026 “I’m going to pick Denver just because of the continuity,” ‘Chucky’ explained. “Head coach [Sean Payton], quarterback [Bo Nix], almost all their starters are back on both sides of the ball, and they’re going to get a jolt from [wide receiver Jaylen] Waddle. I like the Chargers in second, and I like the Chiefs to finish third. But I think all three of those teams can be playoff teams, and I think the Raiders are going to improve. But unfortunately for the Silver and Black, this is a very tough division with some established coaches and quarterbacks.” Gruden’s comments are fair and shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. It’s no secret that 2026 is expected to be a rebuilding year in Las Vegas, as the team pivoted to a youth movement in the offseason. Also, the AFC West has routinely been one of the best divisions in the NFL over the last few years. So, the former head coach isn’t off the mark, as most people seem to expect to see improvement from the Raiders despite the team not improving its standing in the division from last year. In Other Raiders’ Links: Raiders pushing for All-Pros: “[Brock] Bowers is not without competition as Cardinals’ Trey McBride, Chiefs’ Travis Kelce, Falcons’ Kyle Pitts, and 49ers George Kittle all earned All-Pro honors last year,” S&BP’s Tristen Kuhn wrote. “McBride is coming off back to back 1200+ yard seasons, Kelce remains one of the better tight ends in the NFL with top name recognition.” 3 Key aspects to watch during training camp: “The big early training camp questions will be about star defensive end Maxx Crosby, free-agent addition, linebacker Nakobe Dean and rookie cornerback Jermod McCoy. They missed all or most of the offseason sessions,” S&BP’s Bill Williamson wrote. “The team has said they expect them all to be ready for training camp fairly early on.” Bowers gets engaged: The tight end proposed to his girlfriend, now fiancée, Cameron Newell ahead of reporting to training camp. Congrats to the soon-to-be Bowers! Open practice: “The Silver and Black will be in Allegiant Stadium for an open to the public practice on Aug. 11 at 6 p.m. PT. Tickets are $5 each with all proceeds going to the Raiders Foundation ,” via Rachel Gossen of the team’s website .

summary: The Miami Dolphins head into their 2026 training camp with four quarterbacks on the roster: Malik Willis, Quinn Ewers, Cam Miller, and rookie Mark Gronowski. According to a report from NBC Houston’s Aaron Wilson, they may not be done tinkering with the group. According to Wilson, Miami is expected to workout free agent quarterback Jack […]
full_text: DAYTONA BEACH, FLORIDA - JUNE 07: Jack Plummer #13 of the Orlando Storm warms up prior to a game against the DC Defenders at Daytona Stadium on June 07, 2026 in Daytona Beach, Florida. (Photo by Dustin Markland/UFL/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins head into their 2026 training camp with four quarterbacks on the roster: Malik Willis, Quinn Ewers, Cam Miller, and rookie Mark Gronowski. According to a report from NBC Houston’s Aaron Wilson, they may not be done tinkering with the group. According to Wilson, Miami is expected to workout free agent quarterback Jack Plummer next week. Plummer, who went undrafted out of Louisville in 2024, spent most of his rookie season on the Carolina Panthers’ practice squad. After sitting out for the 2025 season, Plummer joined the Orlando Storm of the United Football League in 2026, throwing 2,188 yards with 17 touchdowns, one interception, and a 104.2 passer rating. His passing yards and rating were both league highs, while his passing touchdowns were the second most in the league. The San Francisco 49ers had a workout with Plummer earlier this week. Plummer, no relation to former Pro Bowl quarterback Jake Plummer, started his college career at Purdue for four years before transferring to California. He transferred again a year later, finishing his last season at Louisville. He led Louisville to the 2023 ACC Championship game, losing to Florida State, and the Holiday Bowl, losing to USC. If Plummer impresses in his workout, he could find himself in competition with Ewers, Miller, and Gronowski for a backup role behind presumed starter Willis. The Dolphins’ general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan has said his ideal is to “invest” in the quarterback position every year, with the team looking to draft a quarterback every year or two. The team did not select a passer in this year’s draft, but it appears the team is not done looking for players at the position.

title: Vikings Middle of the Pack in Under-25 Talent
summary: Over the past few years, the Minnesota Vikings’ draft classes have not been highly lauded. That’s largely what led to the firing of GM Kwesi Adofo-Mensah in late January and the odd situation that the Vikings went through during the 2026 offseason prior to Nolan Teasley’s hiring last month. Given that, you would think that […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - DECEMBER 8: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings looks on in the fourth quarter of the game against the Atlanta Falcons at U.S. Bank Stadium on December 8, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The Vikings defeated the Falcons 42-21. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Over the past few years, the Minnesota Vikings’ draft classes have not been highly lauded. That’s largely what led to the firing of GM Kwesi Adofo-Mensah in late January and the odd situation that the Vikings went through during the 2026 offseason prior to Nolan Teasley’s hiring last month. Given that, you would think that the Vikings would rank fairly low in terms of younger talent on the roster, but according to the folks from ESPN, that’s not the case. They’ve racked and stacked all 32 NFL teams in terms of under-25 talent, and the Vikings find themselves in the top half of the league. Not only that, but they’re actually ahead of some of their more highly praised NFC North brethren. The Vikings come in at #13 on ESPN’s list of under-25 talent around the league, which is a nice step up from the #21 spot they occupied on this same list last season. Here’s what they had to say about the purple. Last year’s rank: 21 Blue chips: G Donovan Jackson , Edge Dallas Turner Notable graduated players: K Will Reichard Left guard Jackson, age 23, is one of many top Vikings players, and Turner, also 23, moves into the starting lineup full time this season. First-round rookie defensive tackle Caleb Banks and second-round rookie linebacker Jake Golday also join the 23 club. I wouldn’t really call quarterback J.J. McCarthy a top Vikings player, as he is in a battle with Kyler Murray for the starting spot, but McCarthy is also 23. Jordan Addison , one of the best No. 2 receivers in the NFL, is 24. If Banks hits the way he can hopefully hit, the Vikings will likely move up this list significantly next year. Of course, he’s going to have to be able to stay on the field in order to make that happen, so we’ll have to see how that goes. Jackson and Turner getting recognition is nice to see, too. Addison is going to age off the list next season. As far as the NFC North goes, the Chicago Bears are going to be a problem for a little bit, as they’re way up at #3 on this list. If you want to find the other two NFC North teams, you need to scroll for a bit. The Detroit Lions are down at #23 after being up at #6 on last year’s list, while the Green Bay Packers are ranked at #30. I guess Adofo-Mensah didn’t leave the cupboard completely bare when he left, although he obviously didn’t leave it as full as we would have liked. Hopefully the Nolan Teasley Era will bring about a significant change as far as bringing young talent onto the roster for the foreseeable future.

title: Mike Vrabel keeps mum on Harold Landry’s injury status
summary: Five players were absent from the New England Patriots’ first training camp practice on Saturday, including starting outside linebacker Harold Landry. The team captain had been placed on the physically unable to perform list leading up to camp, and his status remains unclear. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mike Vrabel was unable to give any […]
full_text: Feb 8, 2026; Santa Clara, CA, USA; New England Patriots linebacker Harold Landry III (2) warms up before the game against the Seattle Seahawks in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images | Darren Yamashita-Imagn Images Five players were absent from the New England Patriots’ first training camp practice on Saturday, including starting outside linebacker Harold Landry. The team captain had been placed on the physically unable to perform list leading up to camp, and his status remains unclear. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mike Vrabel was unable to give any concrete updates either. In fact, the Patriots’ head coach even refrained from ruling out the issue impacting Landry’s regular season availability. “I’m not going to predict that. I’m not going to pretend to predict that,” Vrabel said. “Where Harold is at the start of the season, I wouldn’t be able to tell you right now. He won’t be practicing, but he’ll be working, and hopefully we’ll get him back.” Landry arrived in New England last offseason on a three-year, $43.5 million contract. He had an encouraging start to his first season with the club , but a knee injury kept bothering him down the stretch. After playing 78.7% of defensive snaps and registering 6.5 sacks and a forced fumble over the first half of the season, he was limited to 33.8% and two quarterback takedowns after playing through the knee injury in a Week 12 contest versus the Bengals. In total, he finished his first season with 18 games and a 56.7% playing time share. Landry was a limited during offseason workouts earlier this spring, and did not participate during any of the three mandatory minicamp practices. For his coach, this is all part of the unfortunate nature of the game. “We’re going to talk about injuries that could happen, they’re 100% in football,” Vrabel explained. “At some point and time everybody’s going to get hurt. The expectation is they all work extremely hard to get back. That they’re where they’re supposed to be when they’re supposed to be there. They focus on what they can do as opposed to what they can’t do. I’m very confident with our return‑to‑play.” Vrabel and the other players on the PUP or non-football injury lists — RB Terrell Jennings, TE C.J. Dippre, S Brenden Schooler — can be activated at any point during training camp.

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Offense looking for increased urgency
summary: The New England Patriots’ training camp is underway. And while the first session was ultimately relatively uneventful, it was a first dipping of the toes into the 2026 waters for players, fans and media alike. The tempo and intensity will obviously increase in the coming days and weeks, especially following the introduction of full pads. […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye (10) signals to teammates at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots’ training camp is underway. And while the first session was ultimately relatively uneventful, it was a first dipping of the toes into the 2026 waters for players, fans and media alike. The tempo and intensity will obviously increase in the coming days and weeks, especially following the introduction of full pads. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Offensive urgency Despite the success the Patriots offense enjoyed in 2025, mostly in the regular season, it was still the first year of quarterback Drake Maye leading the Josh McDaniels-led unit. Now in their second season together, the hope is for the operation to become smoother, more efficient and: faster. “Just continue to try to operate, be more urgent, get everybody functioning just a little bit quicker,” said head coach Mike Vrabel. “We want to go fast, whether we huddle or we go on the ball. Whatever that looks like, we want to be able to try to dictate the defense a little bit. The urgency in which we operate is something we’ve all talked about; the communication, always taking care of the ball.” A faster operation should allow the Patriots to increase their number of snaps per game, and thus their ability to score points. Last season, despite ranking second in the league in scoring, New England ranked only 18th in plays per game (61.4). That number is influenced by a variety of factors, but a speedier operation is part of it. “We did a lot of great things on offense. We had a bunch of statistics, we did a bunch of things high in the league. We could even create more plays, snap the ball earlier in the play clock and get some things going,” said Maye. “Getting us in the right play first. Getting set under center. Getting ready to get it in the gun. Just moving faster. We got a good play that we like against the defense, just train our guys to be, ‘Hey, once we get down on the football and get set, we’re going.’” Increased stability The Patriots did not have perfect attendance for their first practice of the summer on Saturday, but what they did have is more stability. Comparing the active rosters from the opening day of the team’s 2026 and 2025 training camps, we can see that 44 players are still around. That marks a slight increase compared to the previous two years: only 36 players remained on the team between 2024 and 2025. That increase did not happen by accident. Last summer, after all, was Mike Vrabel’s first as head coach. He overhauled the roster significantly in Year 1 — a process that has slightly slowed down but, as evidenced by the still high turnover rate, remains ongoing. N.C. sessions Whether or not it will become an annual tradition remains to be seen. For a second straight offseason, however, Drake Maye invited some of his teammates to North Carolina for a throwing session before training camp. “We had the guys come to North Carolina again like last year,” Maye said on Saturday. “Got on the lake and got three days of work. It was good to have those guys there, and I think it’s huge in the offseason, right before camp, to get guys going and have them. I feel like we had a good group, some good sessions and it was fun work.” Among the participants was Patriots offseason signing Romeo Doubs. “Just going out there for those few days with Drake and the other guys, getting together and building more chemistry, that’s the norm around this league,” the former Packers wide receiver said. “It was an amazing session that we all had together when we were out there.” Page turned The Patriots’ 2025 season was a success as a whole, but it ultimately ended with a disappointing performance and defeat in the Super Bowl. There is no dwelling on the past, though, as the AFC champions begin their training camp. “Obviously, you play so late and then you lose a big game like that and something you dream about, obviously was hard for a long time,” said tight end Hunter Henry. “But once we got back here, we were able to get to work on this year and what’s ahead. I think we’re all excited for just this year and not really worried about last year.” Rookie signing speed Even though his contract is not yet officially signed, second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas and New England have finally agreed to terms on his rookie deal . This made Jacas the second-to-last player drafted this year to agree to his pact — Rams QB Ty Simpson did the same a few hours later — and the latest to do so among all Patriots draftees since the introduction of the rookie wage scale in 2012. In total, between the first and last reported signings, 78 days passed. The previously longest such stretch for the team was 72 days in 2018, according to calculations by Patriots salary cap expert Miguel Benzan. DeAndre Hopkins’ presence The Patriots’ staff has a new, if temporary, member: five-time All-Pro DeAndre Hopkins joined the team in an assistant capacity, as head coach Mike Vrabel announced ahead of training camp . Hopkins will be around the coaches and the personnel staff, and on Saturday got his first taste of New England practice life. Hopkins spent the session assisting the wide receivers. “It’s really good,” said Romeo Doubs. “It’s my first time seeing DHop in person. I know he’s been an amazing receiver in this league. So, just to have his aura, his energy around is also a huge help, just in our offense. It feels good to be around [him].” Boston College insight The Patriots made a handful of transactions leading up to training camp, and one of those increased the number of Boston College alums on the team’s roster. After previously selecting edge defender Quintayvious Hutchins in the seventh round of the draft, the team has now also signed rookie free agent tight end Jeremiah Franklin. “I have a lot of respect for [Bill O’Brien] at Boston College,” said Mike Vrabel. “Jeremiah is someone we had at local day — we looked at him a lot. The numbers were probably not in his favor at the time and then now I think they are a little bit more favorable. We’re able to bring him in. I think he’s continued to improve. It looked like he’d been working out. I think he’s gotten stronger since March. “Certainly with Q, on the edge, we’re always looking for young pash rushers that can help you. Those guys will have to learn special teams pretty quickly given their body types. That process has already started for Q and Jeremiah will start that process [Saturday].” Hutchins and Franklins are the second and third Eagles on the Patriots’ current roster, joining last year’s free agency pickup Harold Landry. For Vrabel, the connections to the school go beyond those three players, though. His son Tyler spent his four-year college career at B.C. as well. Logan Mankins honored Even though he has yet to make his way into the Patriots Hall of Fame, despite multiple times as a finalist, Logan Mankins remains undisputed as one of the best offensive linemen to ever wear the team’s colors. The same is true at his college, Fresno State. And unlike the Patriots, the Bulldogs have taken the steps to honor the now-44-year-old among the top players in program history: in October, Mankins’ name will be added to the Fresno State Ring of Honor. title: What claiming Kobe Prentice, waiving Sebastian Gutierrez means for the Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots were quite busy on Saturday. Not only did they hold their first practice of this year’s training camp and finally break the contract stalemate with second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas, they also made some roster moves: wide receiver Kobe Prentice was claimed after getting waived by the Panthers, while waiving offensive […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots offensive lineman Jacob Rizy (64) and offensive tackle Sebastian Gutierrez (61) work with coaching staff at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots were quite busy on Saturday. Not only did they hold their first practice of this year’s training camp and finally break the contract stalemate with second-round draft pick Gabe Jacas , they also made some roster moves : wide receiver Kobe Prentice was claimed after getting waived by the Panthers, while waiving offensive tackle Sebastian Gutierrez in a follow-up transaction. Let’s analyze what the moves mean for the club. More speed Checking in at 5-foot-10, 184 pounds, Prentice is not the most physically imposing player. Where he wins and was able to produce a 26-catch, 380-yard, six-touchdown season during his senior year at Baylor, is due to his speed. His 14.6 yards per reception already suggest it: he can get down the field in a hurry. In fact, the 4.37-second 40-yard dash he ran at his Pro Day would have ranked him sixth among wide receivers at the Scouting Combine this year. Overall, it ranks him in the 96th percentile among all wideout prospects over the last 40 years. Another slot New England waived fellow another rookie wide receiver, Jimmy Kibble, with an injury designation on Friday (and he has since reverted to the club’s injured reserve). However, Prentice is not the same type of player: whereas Kibble projected as more of a Z-receiver in the NFL, the newest Patriot was a slot in college and will be a slot as a pro. As such, he will mostly provide depth behind the club’s current top slot, DeMario Douglas. In total, 12 wide receivers are now under contract in New England: Wide receiver (12): A.J. Brown (1), Romeo Doubs (87), DeMario Douglas (3), Kayshon Boutte (9), Mack Hollins (13), Kyle Williams (18), Efton Chism III (86), Jeremiah Webb (29), Kyle Dixon (83), Nick DeGennaro (23), Cameron Dorner (88), Kobe Prentice (—) IR (1): Jimmy Kibble Prentice will be facing an uphill climb to make the roster, especially as part of a deep wide receiver group. What might help his chanced would be the kicking game, but he played no special teams snaps in college. OT depth intact Even though Gutierrez is now on to the waiver wire, the Patriots have plenty of depth at the offensive tackle position. Seven players remain signed at the spot, including three who can be considered roster locks: starters Will Campbell and Morgan Moses as well as first-round rookie Caleb Lomu. Offensive tackle (7): Will Campbell (66 | LT), Morgan Moses (76 | RT), Caleb Lomu (74), James Hudson III (51), Marcus Bryant (52), Lorenz Metz (72), Dametrious Crownover (68) During Saturday’s practice, which might not necessarily be an accurate reflection of the pecking order, the Patriots used both James Hudson and Marcus Bryant as the next men up behind the top three. Gutierrez, meanwhile, ran with the depth players as he did all spring. His release did therefore not come as a surprise, even if it means that Minot State now has no players on an active NFL roster at the moment. No cap impact We covered several Patriots transactions over the last week, and they all had one thing in common: they did not impact New England’s salary cap in any way. Today’s are no exception. Gutierrez was on a one-year, $1.08 million deal that was no high enough to qualify for Top 51 status and included no guarantees of any kind. Prentice’s UDFA deal with the Panthers did include a $15,000 signing bonus prorated over three years, but that money will remain in Carolina; what transfers to New England is his non-guaranteed salaries including $885,000 in 2026. The Patriots therefore are still $34.2 million under the cap right now.

title: Patriots claim former Panthers wide receiver Kobe Prentice, waive tackle
summary: A 12th wide receiver is inbound to Foxborough. The New England Patriots announced the claiming of rookie wideout Kobe Prentice off waivers on Saturday, as previously reported by KPRC 2’s Aaron Wilson. The organization waived offensive tackle Sebastian Gutierrez in a corresponding move following the first practice of training camp. Prentice, 22, entered the NFL […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Charlotte, NC, USA; Carolina Panthers wide receiver Kobe Prentice (39) watches the ball into his hands during the first day of mini camp at Bank of America Stadium practice facility. Mandatory Credit: Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images | Jim Dedmon-Imagn Images A 12th wide receiver is inbound to Foxborough. The New England Patriots announced the claiming of rookie wideout Kobe Prentice off waivers on Saturday, as previously reported by KPRC 2’s Aaron Wilson . The organization waived offensive tackle Sebastian Gutierrez in a corresponding move following the first practice of training camp. Prentice, 22, entered the NFL with the Carolina Panthers as an undrafted free agent in May. The 5-foot-10, 184-pound target landed on the wire to begin the weekend. A former four-star recruit, Prentice played in 36 games at Alabama before transferring to Baylor and adding 11 appearances as a senior. Making four starts between the SEC and the Big 12, his collegiate run spanned 86 receptions for 1,160 yards and 11 touchdowns. Gutierrez, 28, returned to Gillette Stadium on a futures contract in February. The 6-foot-5, 308-pound tackle logged a series of stints on New England’s practice squad dating back to 2022, including re-signings last September and January. Beginning his NFL journey with the Denver Broncos as an undrafted free agent out of Minot State, Gutierrez has twice served as a standard elevation while making additional stops with the Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers, Las Vegas Raiders, Cleveland Browns and Indianapolis Colts. The Patriots move deeper into the summer with an active receiver room that also includes A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, Kayshon Boutte, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III, Jeremiah Webb, Kyle Dixon, Nick DeGennaro and Cameron Dorner. But a recent departure from the depth chart will be remaining in the fold for now. Rookie wideout Jimmy Kibble cleared waivers and reverted to New England’s injured reserve, per the transaction wire. Kibble, 22, had been waived with an injury designation on the eve of camp’s initial practice. Barring an injury settlement at a later date, the move ends his season in July. The 6-foot-1, 199-pound Georgetown product appeared in 39 games during his Hoyas career on the way to catching 149 passes for 2,642 yards and 16 touchdowns. As a team captain in 2025, Kibble totaled 63 receptions for 1,002 yards and four touchdowns en route to first-team All-Patriot League recognition. Amid the roster shuffle, free-agent wide receivers Keagan Johnson and Casey Washington visited Gillette Stadium for workouts on Saturday.

title: Patriots’ Jared Wilson focused on communication in return to center position
summary: As New England Patriots center Jared Wilson transitions back to the middle of the formation in 2026 after spending his rookie season at left guard, communication is vital to building chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye. “The snap and communication,” Wilson said after Saturday’s training camp practice, of what he feels is important in that development. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - MAY 27: Mike Onwenu #71 of the New England Patriots and Jared Wilson #55 of the New England Patriots during New England Patriots OTA on May 27, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images As New England Patriots center Jared Wilson transitions back to the middle of the formation in 2026 after spending his rookie season at left guard, communication is vital to building chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye. “The snap and communication,” Wilson said after Saturday’s training camp practice , of what he feels is important in that development. “First it’s communication, then you’ve got to get the ball to [Maye].” Wilson, a center in college at Georgia, originally repped at the position during training camp last year; however, after frequent mishaps delivering the ball to Maye, he switched to guard, with Garrett Bradbury taking over the reins at the heart of the interior. Now, with Bradbury traded to the Bears and the signing of Alijah Vera-Tucker to be the starting left guard, Wilson has reverted to center. Head coach Mike Vrabel was asked about what he looks for in the chemistry between a quarterback and his center. “Well, I think just the unspoken communication to be able to see it quickly, see it the same [as the quarterback], see it very similar, whether that’s pressure or defensive front, to be able to set the defense or get us in the right play,” Vrabel said. “Communication. I think that the center is the conduit to the rest of the offensive line. “So, when the quarterback needs to get something to the line, the center is the easiest way to get it. And then his communication with everybody else has to be great. So, we’re looking forward to seeing Jared in that transition, working with Drake.” Maye’s and Wilson’s cohesion with one another carries significant weight in the fluency of the offense’s progressions next season. This offseason, New England’s signal-caller has seen Wilson take strides in his communication. “Now you’ve got to be loud; you’ve got to communicate. It’s hard to do. So I think [Wilson’s] done a great job just getting used to the little things at center and how he likes to do the cadence and stuff like that,” Maye said of Wilson’s improved communication. “But we’ve got a great deal with cadence and all that.” Though, their chemistry isn’t perfect just yet. The duo mishandled a snap during Saturday’s practice as Maye continues to learn how Wilson likes to play the position. “[Jared] hasn’t played center for a year, so you get to know his little things,” Maye said. “What he likes, how things work, if he’s going left and I’m going right, how it works, and some of the under-center things.” Each of Wilson’s and Maye’s North Carolina backgrounds may help the duo progress quickly in their chemistry with one another. Out of high school, Maye connected with Wilson through social media, recruiting him to play at UNC. Eventually, Wilson committed to the university in April of 2020, poised to become Maye’s center roughly half a decade ago. That said, Wilson later flipped his commitment to Georgia five months later. The 23-year-old said the two frequently talk about their past all the time, and were during Saturday’s practice. “Very fortunate. It was always meant to be,” Wilson said about being teammates with Maye. “That’s my guy. He’s such a good dude, laid-back dude.”

title: Christian Gonzalez practice participation draws praise from Patriots teammates
summary: As Christian Gonzalez took the field for Day 1 of New England Patriots training camp, he did so without a contract extension.  That did not stop him from participating in full. It also did not stop Drake Maye, who was looking to start training camp with a bang, from testing the No. 1 cornerback immediately.  […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft speaks to cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images As Christian Gonzalez took the field for Day 1 of New England Patriots training camp , he did so without a contract extension. That did not stop him from participating in full. It also did not stop Drake Maye, who was looking to start training camp with a bang, from testing the No. 1 cornerback immediately. Lined up across from A.J. Brown on the team’s first 11-on-11 play, Gonzalez saw Maye’s pass intended for the star receiver hit the turf. “I think that shows his main focus, and that’s football. He’s the best corner in the league in my opinion. He’s not the big rah-rah guy. He does it his own way, but he does it at the highest level. So I’m glad to be his teammate,” Maye said. “Gonzo is someone I look up to even at the same age. I look up to how he does things, how he handles himself, and just his swagger he has in his own way. I think it’s great to see him out here playing around. And I think you saw it in the locker room before. “Everybody was wondering, ‘What’s Gonzo gonna do?’ And he’s coming out here and first play he’s guarding A.J. in man coverage.” Gonzalez’s participation level was a change from this past spring. During mandatory minicamp, the cornerback watched from the sideline once practice shifted to full-team periods. As Maye noted, Gonzalez’s participation level while awaiting a lucrative contract extension was one of the biggest storylines entering training camp. On Day 1, he answered those questions by participating fully. “He’s a team guy, and he’s not gonna let whatever’s going on, you know, he’s out here with us,” cornerback Carlton Davis said. “That’s all I can say about that is he’s out here with us, and he’s always been a good guy. He’s always been a team player.” “That’s just who he is,“ added Milton Williams. ”He want to be here and he’s showing up for us even though he’s got his situation going on. But he’s letting everyone know that he wants to be here and I feel like the contract will handle itself.“ Prior to practice beginning, owner Robert Kraft shared that the team had offered Gonzalez an extension that would pay him as the highest paid cornerback in league history — which would then make him the highest paid Patriot of all-time. Gonzalez’s play has been worthy of that status, while his participation on Saturday may hint that the sides are closing in on an agreement. “He’s definitely one of the best corners in the league and definitely deserves to be paid as such,” Davis said. “So, yeah, he’s deserving of all of it.”

title: 5 performances of note from the Patriots’ first training camp practice
summary: The New England Patriots entered the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Saturday for their first practice of training camp. It was an eventful start to the summer for the reigning AFC champions. To recap the action, please make sure to check out our Patriots training camp notebook. In the meantime, here is who caught our […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - JUNE 09: Kayshon Boutte #9 of the Baltimore Orioles sprints during a minicamp at Gillette Stadium on June 09, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots entered the fields behind Gillette Stadium on Saturday for their first practice of training camp. It was an eventful start to the summer for the reigning AFC champions. To recap the action, please make sure to check out our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the 90-minute session. Standout of the day WR Kayshon Boutte: Despite trade rumors and the arrivals of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs, Kayshon Boutte reported to training camp alongside his teammates and quickly showed why he has been one of Drake Maye’s favorite receivers going back to the QB’s rookie season. During early 11-on-11 work, Maye unleashed a deep ball down the left sideline and hit Boutte on a go route for a gain of approximately 40 yards. “It’s nothing new,” Maye said after practice. “You guys have seen it all year last year, and the year before. He just keeps doing things right. I’m proud of him for getting in there, jumping in there. He understands if he’s got something down the sideline, and a ball down the field, that he’s got a chance it’s coming his way. Great catch.” Other performances of note QB Tommy DeVito: The quarterbacks did not get a lot of work on Saturday, but backup Tommy DeVito still managed to produce a rough start. He went 0-for-3 on the day and struggled particularly during his first series on the field. No turnovers are a positive, but that’s about it. WR DeMario Douglas: The momentum train keeps rolling for the Patriots’ fourth-year receiver. After already being actively involved during the spring, Douglas continued to play a sizable role in the team’s passing offense on Day 1 of camp. He hauled in two passes from Drake Maye and was heavily involved as a slot receiver alongside the aforementioned A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs when New England went to 11-personnel. CB Christian Gonzalez: It took exactly one snap for the Patriots’ starts to collide on Saturday. His first pass attempt of the session saw Drake Maye target A.J. Brown with Gonzalez in coverage. The soon-to-be highest-paid cornerback in the NFL , however, was up for the challenge and provided tight man coverage that helped the ball fall to the ground incomplete. Gonzalez was not seriously tested the rest of the session, but he did participate fully which is a positive development after minicamp. S Mike Brown: The Patriots’ offseason pickup saw action with the starter-level defense in nickel packages, serving as the third safety alongside Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson. It’s early, but this usage is a positive for Brown and suggests that he might be more than a special teamer for New England — even though he did get beat by DeMario Douglas at one point. The Patriots will hold their second practice of training camp on Sunday. Gates will open at 9:15 p.m. ET with the session set to start an hour later.

title: Patriots training camp recap: Christian Gonzalez a full participant on Day 1
summary: The New England Patriots kicked off their 2026 training camp on Saturday on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. The 90-minute session did not feature any pads and minimal contact while the focus of the day was the zone run game installation. “There’ll be a few more runs. We have to get into that,” Mike […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez (0) walks to the practice fields at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | Eric Canha-Imagn Images The New England Patriots kicked off their 2026 training camp on Saturday on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. The 90-minute session did not feature any pads and minimal contact while the focus of the day was the zone run game installation. “There’ll be a few more runs. We have to get into that,” Mike Vrabel said before the session. “Admittedly there’ll be more zone runs, to take away some of those double teams that you have and some of the the gap scheme runs. We we’ll save pads for that… So, there’ll be some of that with the outside zone. We’ll work on first and second down. We’ll have tempo.” Here’s what went down throughout the day. Attendance Absentees: ED Gabe Jacas PUP/NFI: RB Terrell Jennings, TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Injuries: N/A Edge rusher Gabe Jacas continued to be away from the team on Saturday, but that may change soon. The Patriots’ second-round draft pick reportedly agreed to terms on his rookie contract earlier in the day, and might therefore make his practice debut before the start of full-pads sessions later in the week. Outside of Jacas and the four players on the injury lists, the Patriots enjoyed perfect attendance on Day 1 of camp. They also suffered no notable injuries. Takeaways Gonzo participates: Shortly after owner Robert Kraft shared that his team had offered Christian Gonzalez a contract extension that would make him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, the 24-year-old was a full participant in Saturday’s session. That was a noteworthy change from the spring, when Gonzalez stayed away from a large portion of voluntary workouts and sat out of full-team drills during mandatory minicamp. It took no time for him to be tested either, as Drake Maye’s first pass of camp went to A.J. Brown with Gonzalez tight in coverage to help force an incompletion. “I think I had too,” Maye said. “One-on-one over there with Gonzo. I was going to try to start off the camp with a little bang.” Aggressive Drake: Outside of testing Gonzalez on his first pass of camp, Drake Maye was aggressive throwing the football in his four periods of work. With a focus on the run installation, Maye threw the ball just nine times in competitive work but quickly delivered the highlight of the day early connecting on a deep ball to a diving Kayshon Boutte. Near the end of his day, Maye seemingly hand-delivered a seam ball to Hunter Henry just on top of Christian Elliss before hitting an open DeMario Douglas over the middle of the field for a chunk gain. Receiver watch: A.J. Brown did not catch a pass on Day 1 of camp while Romeo Doubs and Maye connected on their lone target. But those two were stapled on Maye’s unit for much of the afternoon with DeMario Douglas often being the third receiver in 11-personnel. As Kayshon Boutte worked in with both first and second units (catching just the deep ball from Maye), that left Kyle Williams, Mack Hollins, and Efton Chism III largely serving as Tommy DeVito and Behren Morton’s receivers. Chism hauled in one catch from the latter and saw another open target sail far and high from DeVito. O-line shuffle: The Patriots’ starting offensive line looked as expected with Will Campbell, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, Mike Onwenu, and Morgan Moses aligning as the top unit from left to right. First-round rookie Caleb Lomu received reps as the sixth O-lineman and in place of Moses at right tackle, while veteran offseason signing James Hudson also saw time in that spot. As he ended the spring, Alijah Vera-Tucker participated in full as he works back from last year’s season ending triceps injury. The end of practice also featured a bad snap between Jared Wilson and Maye, which the QB took the blame for. Big Nickel: Carrying over from the spring, the Patriots defense continued to deploy more three-safety packages to open the summer. Joining regular starters Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson in the secondary was free agent addition Mike Brown, who moved into the slot in those looks. Dell Pettus held that role with the second defensive unit and also came onto the field when New England went big nickel. Other notes: Backup QB Tommy DeVito opened with a rough first period as he misfired on all three of his attempts. DeVito settled down a bit in his second session while rookie Behren Morton had several nice completions to Efton Chism and stepping up in the pocket to find Myles Montgomery. Rookie tight end Eli Raridon sparingly worked in with the first unit behind Hunter Henry. His first target came from DeVito and was sailed high up the seam before the duo connected in the next period on a sail route. With Harold Landry and Gabe Jacas sidelined, Dre’Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder continued to work as the top edge defenders. Bradyn Swinson mixed into the group and batted a pass down at the line of scrimmage. As Vrabel hinted at, tempo was a key part of practice for the offense with the unit often hurrying to the line of scrimmage after big plays. Coach DeAndre Hopkins was on scene and worked with the wide receivers ahead of practice. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Sunday for Day 2 of camp which is set to begin at 10:30 a.m. ET.

title: Patriots have record-breaking contract offer on the table for Christian Gonzalez
summary: Christian Gonzalez is one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL, and looking to get compensated accordingly. The New England Patriots, if team owner Robert Kraft is to be believed, want to meet those demands. Speaking to reporters ahead of the Patriots’ first training camp practice on Saturday, Kraft said that the Patriots have a […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA- JUNE 11: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots stretches during New England Patriots Minicamp on June 11, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Christian Gonzalez is one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL, and looking to get compensated accordingly. The New England Patriots, if team owner Robert Kraft is to be believed, want to meet those demands. Speaking to reporters ahead of the Patriots’ first training camp practice on Saturday, Kraft said that the Patriots have a record contract offer on the table for the 24-year-old. “We love Christian Gonzalez. We love him as a player, as a person. That’s why we’ve made an offer to him that makes him the highest-paid player ever to play that position in the NFL,” Kraft told reporters on the Gillette Stadium practice fields. “Coincidentally, it’s the highest contract in Patriots franchise history.” Gonzalez arrived in New England as the 17th overall selection in the 2023 NFL Draft, and since then has been a mainstay in the team’s secondary. A one-time Pro Bowler and one-time All-Pro, he was arguably the club’s most consistent performer the last two seasons and has established himself among the elite players at the cornerback position. He did all that while still on his rookie contract. The Patriots did exercise the fifth-year option in his contract earlier this offseason but Gonzalez is looking for a longer-term commitment than through the 2027 season. That is also what the organization is looking for, according to Kraft. 2We’re glad we drafted him and he’s developed here, and we hope he will be with us for a long time,” he said. Trent McDuffie currently holds the title as the highest-paid cornerback in football. The 26-year-old signed a four-year, $124 million contract extension earlier this offseason shortly after getting traded from the Chiefs to the Rams. The expectation is that Gonzalez as well as fellow 2023 first-round draft pick Devon Witherspoon will both surpass McDuffie’s yearly average of $31 million.

title: Staff Focus: Kellen Moore and the coordinators
summary: Much of the focus is on the New Orleans Saints’ players, which absolutely makes sense, but the coaching staff also should be discussed. Their influence can sometimes be overlooked, but ultimately, this group are those people who keep everything together and lead the team to success. So, let’s look at where Kellen Moore and the […]
full_text: Dec 21, 2025; New Orleans, Louisiana, USA; New Orleans Saints head coach Kellen Moore is seen before a game against the New York Jets at Caesars Superdome. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Hinton-Imagn Images | Matthew Hinton-Imagn Images Much of the focus is on the New Orleans Saints’ players, which absolutely makes sense, but the coaching staff also should be discussed. Their influence can sometimes be overlooked, but ultimately, this group are those people who keep everything together and lead the team to success. So, let’s look at where Kellen Moore and the coordinators are currently going headed into training camp. Kellen Moore Starting with the head coach, this is a big year for Kellen Moore. It was definitely not perfect in 2025. While Spencer Rattler was at QB, Moore really struggled with the offensive playcalling, couldn’t trust Rattler, and his situational decision-making was rough at times. The good news was that these were all issues for a first-time head coach and as long as they improved over the season, all was well. For Moore, it wasn’t perfect, but he did just that, improved. Once Tyler Shough was in at QB, it was clear the trust Moore had in him, and the playcalling improved substantially, but the decision-making during situational moments was still a bit questionable. Moore overcame so much in his first year with the Saints, so hopefully that issue can be fixed; otherwise, the Saints will be losing close games. Brandon Staley Probably the MVP of the coaching staff, Brandon Staley had an excellent first year in New Orleans. The defense was definitely not a perfect group on paper, and at times during the season, they showed that, but Staley had this defense playing at a high level. They were the strength of the team in 2025. What’s going to be interesting for 2026 is if Staley can do that again. After losing some players in free agency but signing others, the team is at a very similar spot to where they were last season. With the investments the Saints made on offense, that side of the ball is probably going to be the strength of the team, but Staley could do some magic and elevate this defense even more. That may cause him to leave for an head coaching job sooner rather than later. Doug Nussmeier This section will be a bit quicker because Doug Nussmeier, the offensive coordinator, and Kellen Moore are in the same boat. Both are focused on offense, and Nussmeier needs to help Moore perform better in key moments. They are a team inside of this team. The one difference would be that I can’t wait to see Nussmeier helping Shough develop even more. When we look at what Shough has done this season, praise will be given to this offensive staff, built to develop QBs. Phil Galiano Last, but certainly not least, is Phil Galiano. Special teams was a bit of a mess last season, and most of the blame ended up getting thrown at Galiano because of some of the decision-making, such as not moving on from Blake Grupe faster and cutting Rico Payton before the season, which was questionable. But it’s also important to understand that the entire special teams unit was an issue. The personnel was just not good enough, and that won’t be an issue in 2026. Out of everyone, it does feel like Galiano is the one on the hot seat, because if issues like last season happen again (with a much better group), it may be over.

title: 5 areas where Jaxson Dart needs to improve, and how the Giants can help him do it
summary: Jaxson Dart did enough in his rookie season to make the New York Giants believe they might have found the answer they have been seeking at quarterback since Eli Manning retired. Dart played well enough, in fact, to be one of the reasons why John Harbaugh was interested in taking the Giants’ head-coaching job. “The […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart | Getty Images Jaxson Dart did enough in his rookie season to make the New York Giants believe they might have found the answer they have been seeking at quarterback since Eli Manning retired. Dart played well enough, in fact, to be one of the reasons why John Harbaugh was interested in taking the Giants’ head-coaching job. “The quarterback’s kind of important. You know, that’s kind of a big deal,” Harbaugh said at his introductory press conference. “I’m excited about Jaxson Dart.” After working with the young quarterback for a few months, Harbaugh’s excitement has grown. “I don’t know about surprised, probably just impressed more than anything. I do think he’s obsessed. I believe he really really wants to be good,” Harbaugh said recently via Bleav in Giants with Bob Papa and Carl Banks. “He’s kinda got the it factor from a leadership standpoint because he’s respected by the guys. They just know how hard he works, how much he prepares and they respect his talent. He’s got some charisma.” Dart has all those things. What he doesn’t have are the pelts on the wall that prove he is a top 10-type quarterback the Giants can and will win with on a consistent basis. Quarterback rankings should be taken with a grain of salt. This list of starting quarterback rankings, though, tells a consistent story: Pro Football Focus — Dart is No. 25 SB Nation — Dart is No. 28 Sports Illustrated — Dart is No. 23 FOX Sports — Dart is No. 21 NBC Sports (Chris Simms) — Dart is No. 22 The story those rankings tell? That Dart has a long way to go to become the quarterback the Giants drafted him to be, and think he can be. Simms summarized Dart this way: Dart is a master of backyard football who can make magic happen but questions remain about the quarterback’s ability to thrive in the pocket heading into his second season. The Giants have been here before Not so long ago a rookie quarterback named Daniel Jones excited the fan base by throwing 24 touchdown passes to 12 interceptions while passing for 3,207 yards in 13 games, 12 of them starts. Jones was “Danny Dimes.” He could throw it. He could run it. His rookie season offered hope that GM Dave Gettleman, criticized for using the No. 6 overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft on Jones, would be proven right. That, of course, did not happen. Jones has never again reached 20 touchdown passes in a season. The 2025 season with the Indianapolis Colts is the only time Jones has surpassed the 232.8 yards passing per game that he averaged as a rookie. He averaged 238.5 yards in 13 games. So, as good as most feel about Dart’s future, there are no guarantees. The hoped-for leap into the upper tier of quarterbacks never truly happened for Jones. Will it happen for Dart? The New York Post did some Year 2 quarterback research that bodes well for Dart : The Post researched the 33 first-round quarterbacks drafted from 2016-24 to see how many actually took a Year 2 leap — or was it more like a baby step? — and how many went in the other direction. Removing five instances where there is not enough data over the first two seasons to draw a conclusion, 19 of the other 28 experienced a spike in quarterback rating, including seven whose progress was dramatic. Of the nine who went in reverse, only one (the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels) was limited by injury. But perhaps the most interesting finding related to expectations for Dart in 2026 is that quarterbacks who had a new head coach and new offensive coordinator made some of the biggest strides. The Post pointed to Drake Maye of the New England Patriots and Caleb Williams of the Chicago Bears as examples of the quarterback/new coach jump. Young quarterback issues Young quarterbacks in the NFL always have a lot to learn. The variety of things Dart needs to improve upon appear to be things typical of quarterbacks early in their NFL careers. Let’s break these down into a handful of categories. In reality, as you will see, the various categories overlap in some ways. Too much hero ball This is really the “Dart takes too many hits when he runs” category. The Giants can’t take running the ball out of Dart’s game, it is part of what makes him dynamic. Per Sumer Sports, Dart was third in the NFL in quarterback rush yards (487), second in rushing touchdowns (9), and second in Expected Points Added (EPA) when running (38.12). Harbaugh has no intention of taking that away from his quarterback . As has been discussed ad nauseum, what the Giants need Dart to do when he does run is to protect himself, to make smarter decisions about when to put the ball and his body at risk. As a rookie, Dart seemed resistant to the idea that discretion was the better part of valor. The unnecessary hit that he took against the New England Patriots after missing two games with a concussion is evidence of that. The fight that broke out after Patriots LB Christian Elliss hit Jaxson Dart (🎥: @espn ) pic.twitter.com/0vKvKPWRju — Complex Sports (@ComplexSports) December 2, 2025 Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan have spent time showing Dart clips and going over when it is and is not worth taking risks. Callahan said there have been some “very direct conversations” with Dart about things he needs to improve upon. One of those, of course, is not subjecting himself to unnecessary hits. “There’s an awareness of when to put yourself at risk, when to get out of bounds, when to get down on the ground and not take a hit, and when to be smart with the football,” Callahan said. “Those are things you just point out … but I never want to take that ability to affect the game with his legs because it’s something that makes him a really dangerous player.” Dart sounds like he has gotten the message . “It’s important for the quarterback to make sure how he’s feeling one play that he’s going to feel that same way the next play,” Dart said this spring. “And at the same time, just having the experience last year of sitting out two games, I hadn’t done that in my career. So, I just hated that time of not being out there with my teammates. So obviously I understand the most important thing is to be out there. So, you just grow and learn from things. And I think I’m going to do a good job at it this year for sure. “My competitiveness isn’t going to change at all. I think, just like I said, it just goes into situationally. Just what times it’s worth it and what times it’s not. And just making those mature decisions.” We will see if words lead to actions. Not always making the right read Greg Cosell, one of the premier quarterback analysts in the business, said recently of Dart that “there were times he didn’t see it the right way” during his rookie season. Cosell told Ross Tucker that Dart will “get better in that regard with more experience.” “Jaxson Dart had a solid rookie season…” “There were times he didn't SEE it the right way. And when quarterbacks can run, when they don't see it the right way, they TAKE OFF…” @GregCosell breaks down the Giants QB going into Year 2: pic.twitter.com/AE8YtdXIgj — Ross Tucker Podcast (@RossTuckerPod) July 16, 2026 One of Dart’s strengths is, of course, his ability to make plays with his legs. Cosell pointed out that this is a double-edged sword for young quarterbacks that often causes them to run before they need to. “When quarterbacks can run, when they don’t see it the right way, they take off,” Cosell said. “And that disrupts your pass game and obviously as we saw last year, it caused problems for him in terms of injury.” According to Pro Football Focus, Dart was the worst quarterback in the league last season in terms of allowed pressure — defined as pressures where the quarterback is fully or partly responsible for being pressured while attempting to pass. Dart was at least partly responsible 39.1% of the time when pressured. Shedeur Sanders was second at 27.3%. Dart was at least partially at fault on 50 pressures. Only Maye (52) was responsible for more. Maye’s total,…

title: Survey results: Fans are intrigued by the cornerback competition
summary: Football is almost back and the New York Giants will be opening their first training camp under John Harbaugh next week. The return of football is always an exciting time, and this year’s camp offers an extra helping (or two) of intrigue. Not only do we get the usual curiosity as to what the coming […]
full_text: The New York Giants 2026 rookie class before practice. | John Jones-Imagn Images Football is almost back and the New York Giants will be opening their first training camp under John Harbaugh next week. The return of football is always an exciting time, and this year’s camp offers an extra helping (or two) of intrigue. Not only do we get the usual curiosity as to what the coming year’s team will look, but the new regime under Harbaugh offers several layers of intrigue. Not only do we not know what the new offensive and defensive schemes will look like, we also don’t know exactly what the final roster will look like. Training camps always feature position battles, but a host of clean slates and some roster turnover has created more uncertainty than usual. This week we asked you which position battle you’re most interested in seeing. And while cornerback won the poll, the results are interesting across the board. It does make sense that the battle for the starting cornerback job opposite Paulson Adebo is the most intriguing to fans. After all, the defense has been the biggest pain point for a while now, particularly considering how many times the defense snatched defeat from the jaws of victory last year. It’s made all the more interesting by the fact that the position battle seems to be a straight ahead duel between Gregory Newsome II and Deonte Banks, while rookie Colton Hood develops on the second team. Both Newsome and Banks are former first round picks who flashed upside early in their careers but have since regressed. Fans want to see whether the defensive staff can get one (or both) to play up to their potential and become gems for the defense. It’s both interesting and expected that wide receiver took the second spot. There are far more questions than answers at the position, with intrigue at just about every level. The Giants have added a bunch of receivers this year, but can any combination of them make opponents fear the Giants’ passing attack? Likewise, how many of the receivers can do enough that Jaxson Dart doesn’t feel as though he needs to win the game on his own? Right now the over-under on Dart’s passing yardage is 3,100.5 per FanDuel . That averages out to just over 182 yards per game. While that would be an improvement over his rookie numbers, that also isn’t going to scare many good defenses. Can an improved receiving corps help the Giants take the NFL (and Vegas) by surprise? At the opposite end of the spectrum, it IS surprising that both defensive line and kicker didn’t get more support. As mentioned above, the defense has been a major pain point for a while now, and the Giants’ defensive line was thrown into turmoil by the loss of Dexter Lawrence (trade), Rakeem Nunez-Roches (free agency), Roy Robertson-Harris (injury), and Sam Roberts (injury). We expect DJ Reader and Darius Alexander to be two starters, but things are fluid and surprises could happen. We also don’t know just how the defensive line will be used and how the players will step up. And considering the Giants have lost multiple games over the last couple years due to uncertainty and inconsistency at kicker, how that battle shakes out could determine the outcome of games. It’s also highly unusual that a team has no experienced veterans competing for the kicker job. The kicker tends to be an afterthought right up until they aren’t. However, it would definitely be news if undrafted rookie Dominic Zvada (who seems to be leading the competition after mini-camp) wins the job and also holds off all the veteran free agents.

title: Explaining NFL roster designations: What PUP, IR, NFI mean
summary: The New York Giants recently placed three players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list in advance of training camp. What do all of the lists/roster designations we commonly hear about mean? Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) The physically unable to perform (PUP) list is for players who are judged physically unable to perform […]
full_text: Thomas Fidone is on the PUP list. | Getty Images The New York Giants recently placed three players on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list in advance of training camp. What do all of the lists/roster designations we commonly hear about mean? Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) The physically unable to perform (PUP) list is for players who are judged physically unable to perform in football activities due to an injury suffered playing or practicing football. Players on the PUP list can be around the team, but cannot practice. Players must be placed on the PUP list before the beginning of training camp. There are two varieties of PUP lists: Active PUP — These are players placed on the PUP list before training camp. They are counted as part of a team’s 90-man roster, but are not allowed to practice until physically cleared and removed from PUP. A player on Active PUP can be removed from the list at any point in training camp. Reserve PUP — If a player on Active PUP during training camp is not removed from the list, he can be placed on this list when teams cut their rosters to the 53-man regular-season limit. A player on this list must miss at least the first four games of the season. One change to this rule for 2026 is that players on Reserve PUP can now begin practicing after missing the first two weeks. Previously, the 21-day practice window to decided whether to activate a player or place him on season-ending Injured Reserve opened after the four-week time frame. Injured Reserve (IR) Players are placed on Injured Reserve (IR) when they suffer a football-related injury that will force them to miss several games, allowing their team to replace them on the roster. NFL rules now allow up to two players who were placed on IR to be designated to return during the season. If a player is placed on IR before roster cutdowns, they are ineligible to return. That is why the Giants, who believe there is a small chance defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris can return this season from his torn Achilles tendon, have not placed Robertson-Harris on IR. Team can designate as many as eight players to return from IR during the season, 10 if they reach the playoffs. Players on IR must miss at least four games. Non-Football Injury/Illness (NFI) The Non-Football Injury (NFI) list pertains to players who were injured or became ill while away from football activities, such as if they were injured working out on their own away from the team facility. The NFI list functions similarly to the PUP list in terms of active and reserve NFI.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Matt Nagy, and a Kevin Zeitler vs. Jon Runyan debate
summary: Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, as a follow up to one of last week’s Mailbag questions, has there been any discussion on where Nagy will be on game day? While I appreciate coordinators getting a bird’s eye view of the field up in the booth, I prefer to see a coach directly interacting with the players on […]
full_text: Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, as a follow up to one of last week’s Mailbag questions, has there been any discussion on where Nagy will be on game day? While I appreciate coordinators getting a bird’s eye view of the field up in the booth, I prefer to see a coach directly interacting with the players on the sideline. I know there is no right/wrong answer, just preferences and coaching styles. What’s your opinion on this and what have you heard from this staff? Ed says: Kölner, I don’t recall any discussion of that. I went back through some of the transcripts, and don’t see it discussed. I do think Matt Nagy’s history is calling plays from the sideline. Here is some really interesting research on the topic: Booth or sideline: where should your team’s play caller be? Inspired by @CoachDanCasey . 20 seasons. 5,431 games. 10,700+ caller-team observations. Offense: Sideline 22.88 PPG | Booth 21.35 Defense: Booth 22.32 PPG allowed | Sideline 22.57 Offense performed better with the play… — Ryan Paganetti (@RyanPaganetti) July 14, 2026 I am a big fan of coaches calling plays from the sideline where they can feel the game and interact personally with the players. FirstWave asks: Please explain why some wide receivers, whether they be younger or older, cannot play special teams? What is prohibiting them? They are football players. Special teams is part of football. Ed says: ‘First’, some wide receivers are really good special teamss players. Dalen Cambre and Ryan Miller on the Giants are good in that area. Ex-Giant Cody Core was really good. Devin Thomas, a wide receiver, was a good special teamer who made a massive fumble recovery for the Giants in the 2012 NFC Championship Game. Steve Tasker was a wide receiver who made the Hall of Fame as a special teams player. Defensive players are generally more used to the contact, the physicality, the tackling that is required. Can you see Jalin Hyatt or 5-foot-9, 162-pound Calvin Austin defeating blockers and making tackles? I can’t. A team could put them out there to cover kicks or punts, but more than likely they would be a liability. It is really about the skillset and mentality. Steve Williams asks: Hi Ed, I have a question regarding Marcus Mbow. Last season he showed promise as a rookie swing tackle and is the likely backup for both Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemenor this year. However, one of the points that several people have recently made was that Mbow needs to increase his play strength along with adding some bulk. Based on the OTA’s this spring, did you see any indication that Mbow has in fact been hitting the weight room and the high-protein dinner table? And does his agility and quickness still look as good as it did at times last year? Ed says: Steve, I seem to get a lot of questions about Mbow and whether or not he looks stronger than he did a year ago. It isn’t really a question I can answer heading into training camp. Remember, there are no pads — thus no hitting — during spring practices. Understand also that media is only at the facility for a maximum of six spring practices — three OTAs and three minicamp workouts. We do not get free reign to speak with whatever players we want, we are at the mercy of the Giants to give us two or three players each day in podium sessions. We have not spoken to Mbow. Whether he has added strength or bulk is something I will try to ascertain as camp moves along. I know there is a lot of interest, and I wish I had something real to tell you guys. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Taj Siddiqi asks: In my mind Micah McFadden is a player who is very good at diagnosing a play yet doesn’t have enough strength to tackle in most cases. I have watched me run over by many RBs. What your experienced eyes tell you about his tackling? Ed says: Taj, you are right to worry about McFadden’s tackling. Per Pro Football Focus, he has a missed tackle rate of 15.6% in his career. That is far too high. I do not think you are right about the cause. In my view, the issue is not strength. I have always said that McFadden gets himself into position to make a lot of plays, then does not make them. To me, the issue is athleticism. I don’t know if it is quickness, ability to change direction or what, but one-on-one in open space I think backs and receivers are able to make him miss too often. Doug Mollin asks: Could we cut Runyan and sign Zeitler with the savings on a one year deal? Zeitler is 36 but he’s started between 15 and 17 games every season since 2015. And he had a 71 PFF run blocking grade and 75 PFF pass blocking grade last year. Zeitler’s a bigger guy than Runyan too — 6’4″ 340 pounds vs 6’4″ 307. I really hope Harbaugh does not have a blind spot about Faalele; he’s here on a minimum contract for a reason. Ed says: Doug, cutting Jon Runyan before the season starts remains a possibility. I don’t think signing Kevin Zeitler to replace him is going to happen. Zeitler has been in the NFL since 2012. He has played two emergency snaps at left guard and two emergency snap at left tackle. He has played 13,991 snaps at right guard. Zeitler is a right guard only, and that position is occupied by Francis Mauigoa. The Giants aren’t moving Mauigoa, and Zeitler will have enough options that he won’t sign somewhere to play his 15th NFL season out of position. Submit a question Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.
